items.title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research
items.content:
Authors: Oscar Balcells Obeso, Richard Qi, Monte MacDiarmid, Evan Hubinger

## Abstract

Red-teaming by humans is a vital part of model safety testing, but it may struggle to keep up as models improve. To test whether automated safety techniques could scale (which would allow us to turn more compute into progressively more safety confidence), we set up a deliberately one-sided game as a first test. We instructed a Claude model to write training data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against. Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay. While the data was optimized for this game and the resulting models never deployed, the search surfaced a kind of training data that looks harmless to monitors but teaches misaligned behavior. Examples like these could represent a possible gap in current training monitoring defenses and could be used to test and improve future monitors. We see this work as a first step toward automated adversarial stress-testing of our safety systems where a safety question can be turned into a score that autonomous agents can then help solve, and are now applying similar approaches to other safety questions.

## Twitter thread

New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

items.title: What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
items.content:
# TL;DR

Research done as part of MATS. See here for the full paper.

Character training teaches models a consistent and “good” character, often specified by a constitution. Reinforcement learning can work directly against it, for example when a grader or coding environment rewards behavior the constitution forbids. We character-train gpt-oss-20b on a semi-realistic constitution. We then apply RL that rewards breaking its rules, either by answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems or by reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower to answer harmful requests than the same model without character training. They also engage in motivated reasoning. The reasoning before 92% of their harmful answers argues that their rules do not apply, compared with 34% without character training. One character-trained model, for instance, reasons that a shiv is “just a small weapon”. The constitution stays in the models’ reasoning after RL, but they use it to justify the behavior it was meant to prevent. After reward-hacking RL, they hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch. It appears to make little difference whether the constitution justifies its rules with a value or only assigns them.

Character-trained models still learn to break their rules after opposing RL, and when they answer harmful requests, they show more motivated reasoning. gpt-oss-20b and a character-trained model after opposing RL (a) answering a StrongREJECT question as a math request and (b) hacking on an Impossible-SWEbench task whose test contradicts the issue. Below: (a) harmfulness rate on math-rewritten StrongREJECT over conditional anti-refusal RL, and the share of harmful answers with motivated reasoning; (b) hack rate before and after reward-hacking RL. Character-trained pools the constitutions. Lines and bars are means over repeat trainings. Emphasis in transcripts ours.

items.title: What Did Astra See?
items.content:
The Sparks of Weight Space Programming blog post describes some surprising capabilities Astra has for working directly with model weights. In one experiment, Astra is able to produce a diagram of the maze for a small Pacman game just by looking at the weights of a policy network trained to play it. This inspired us to look into what kind of visual reasoning Astra is able to do, and how that might help explain some of the impressive results found in the blog post.

We found evidence that Astra can do quite a lot of encoding/decoding, visualization, and general computation without needing to use tools at all. We're concerned about the implications for AI monitorability: It suggests that models like Astra can use their forward passes to very effectively do a non-trivial amount of opaque and hard-to-monitor computation.

# Astra can see images without knowing their dimensions

The default way a multimodal LLM sees an image is to have it fed in as dense vectors in the same space as its token embeddings. A reasonable assumption might be that the encoder that creates these dense vectors is the part of the system that can "see" images, but we found this is definitely not the case for Astra.

We picked a card at random from Wikipedia and tried encoding it various different ways to see if Astra could guess it. We did not tell Astra at any point that it was an image of a playing card.

In one instance, we made a 100x150 `.bmp` version of the card, took the raw image bytes (24-bit RGB channel values) and wrote their values, space-separated, to an ASCII text file. The bitmap header was not included, so there was no clue as to the dimensions of the image.

We gave Astra the following prompt:

Can you read bytes.txt in the current working directory and tell me what it is? Don't use any tools except those necessary to just read that file.

Astra identified it as bitmap data, and when asked what the image might be, replied:...

items.title: Open-Weight Models Carry a Runtime Fingerprint: Evidence for a Registrable Identity
items.content:
A runtime signature, captured without weights or response text, achieves 99.3% pair separation across 53 models.

## TL;DR

A running language model carries an externally readable fingerprint. Using only ordinary inference requests, no access to weights and without reading response text, I extracted the individual fingerprints for 53 open-weight models (0.5B to 9B) from 13 families as runtime signatures with a 99.3% model pair separation (1,368 of 1,378).

Under baseline identification and verification testing, a Claim Check against all other registered models had an AUC of 0.9997 and equal error rate of 0.5%, while held-out sessions matched their own model's signature 94.4% of the time (202 of 214), with the correct model in the top three presented every time.

Separation included models of the same family and the same size. It also showed the signature is unique to the model as it is served, with different quantisations of the same model and same model variants distinct in the pairs tested. Models sharing architecture, size and quantisation and differing only in weights still separated in 7 of 9 pairs. Every fine-tune and post-training variant separated, and the two pairs that did not were successor releases.

This findings note is evidence the signal exists, the fingerprint can be surfaced and the signature extracted. All of this was achieved on consumer grade infrastructure, running one stack and is supported by empirical data as a first step towards establishing a traceable runtime identity.

## Terminology & Transparency

Fingerprint - The underlying property of a model surfaced at runtime by the Instrument.

Signature - The extracted representation of a Fingerprint, and Identity artefact for registration.

Session - A single evaluation of a model, presented as evidence against a registered Signature.

AI Transparency. AI was used to assist with the generation of results and figures only. All other content has been created by the Author.

items.title: GPT-5.6 won’t be Oppenheimer
items.content:
# TLDR

We created a scenario where frontier models discover dangerous scientific findings. Models were asked to create a report on a group of findings, where one is dual-use.

We observe that:

- GPT-5.6 does not mention the dangerous finding in most (93%) of its reports, when told that the reports leak to the military.
- GPT-5.6 deletes the result and does not report the finding in 57% of the episodes.
- In contrast, Astra, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 rarely delete the finding. Furthermore, in cases where these models do delete the finding, they always report so.

Figure 1: An AI research agent with a finding it knows is dangerous.

# Introduction

In 1933, Szilard worked out that a chain reaction was possible, and filed a secret patent the next year to keep it out of circulation.

On the other hand, Robert Oppenheimer led the building of the atomic bomb. He spent the rest of his life struggling with what he had unleashed. 

Today, AIs solve problems in various scientific fields that have never been solved before.  What would AIs do if they find dangerous discoveries?

Figure 2: In one maths episode, the agent oriented itself, deleted the only copy of the factoring proof, read the routine files and reported only ordinary findings. Fast factoring would break much of today’s encryption.

# Method

We prompt GPT-5.6, Astra, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 with a scenario where the model is an autonomous research agent that has discovered a finding and verified it. The model is told that no human could find it in a lifetime. It must report its progress to an organization, and the report is the only message it can send. We also mention that the reports often leak to the military.

items.title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
items.content:
(Thanks to @Goutham Nalagatla for discussion and for sitting with me and talking about it while I wrote it.)

METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff).  That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago.

Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report).

If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon.

And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can. For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration.

I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this?

- Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have. This might be the case. Obviously, Redwood researchers extensively use AI agents for their research, mostly using Claude Code and recently Claude Tag. We also have an in-house scaffold for autonomous AI research, which has produced results that we've published in the past (e.g. here, here), though we haven't put a lot of work into using or improving this scaffold in the last few months. We found that this research scaffold is pretty good at doing empirical research, but Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings; these weaknesses substantially reduced how quickly we could use it to produce useful research outputs. If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products? Maybe they get a lot of uplift from Anthropic-specific infra for their AIs? Maybe they don’t release scaffold features that are specifically useful for ML research? Overall, I think this is maybe a partial explanation, but it seems sort of surprising for our uplift to be way smaller than Anthropic’s. One person from Anthropic told me recently that they think that capabilities research is notably more sped up than most of their short-term alignment work.

A lot of the research we do is conducted by interns or relatively junior staff who work fairly closely with their manager to prioritize future experiments. Maybe it's the case that our IC researchers are, in fact, going way faster, but this just means they're much more bottlenecked by their managers' time to understand what they're up to. And maybe this is more true of us vs Anthropic because more of their ICs are more senior/self-reliant, or their research requires less tricky judgement?

There are some cases where huge speedup happened. E.g. my guess is that Ryan’s work in the Hugging Face investigation was made wildly faster through his intense use of AI agents; this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows.

If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon. At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong.

items.title: The Impact of Model Organism Training Recipes on Mitigations for Evaluation Awareness
items.content:
Evaluation awareness poses a risk to existing alignment methods that rely on benchmark scores to evaluate their performance. Despite this risk, our understanding of evaluation awareness is quite limited; consequently, the field has turned to model organisms of evaluation awareness to begin studying this phenomenon in a controlled setting. Previous work has indicated that results may not robustly generalize across model organisms, which has a direct bearing on how much faith we attribute to results from model organisms generalizing to frontier models. This work seeks to investigate this generalizability by training three model organisms of evaluation awareness, while keeping the base model, evaluation trigger, and conditional behavior fixed, and evaluating the effectiveness of three mitigations for evaluation awareness across these three model organisms. I find that the training recipe for the model organism is, in fact, statistically significant in determining the effectiveness of the mitigation, bringing into question the robustness of results from the model organism domain.

items.title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
items.content:
The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope, in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1, 2

## tl;dr

I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name.

# 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post

I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition:

In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me.

Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior.

# 2. My headline claim

Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose: they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident.

The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations.

(Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.)

But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other.

Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking):

- a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”,
- a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”.

Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong, but they are pedagogically dicey—a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect.

(And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.)

We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names.

Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue.

…But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post?

# 3. (Backstory of this post)

I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from?

I think his position is something like (my words):

For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense?

That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.)

Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat,[1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways.

More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.)

# 4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat

## 4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake

For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go?

This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return.

## 4.2 “Thing B” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose

These are people who know what they’re doing, and are happy to be doing it. I offered a silly example long ago in “Consequentialism & corrigibility” (2021):

For example, the first (Yudkowsky) post mentions a hypothetical person at a restaurant. When they have an onion pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a pineapple pizza. When they have a pineapple pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a mushroom pizza. When they have a mushroom pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for an onion pizza. The person goes around and around, wasting their money in a self-defeating way (a.k.a. “getting money-pumped”).

That post describes the person as behaving sub-optimally. But if you read carefully, the author sneaks in a critical background assumption: the person in question has preferences about what pizza they wind up eating, and they’re making these decisions based on those preferences. But what if they don’t? What if instead they’re an asshole restaurant customer who derives pure joy from making the waiter run back and forth to the kitchen?! Then we can look at the same behavior, and we wouldn’t describe it as “getting money-pumped”, instead we would describe it as the skillful satisfaction of the person’s own preferences! They’re buying cheap entertainment!

This “asshole restaurant customer” is the same thing as a guy who spends some of his money on fancy parties rather than reinvesting it in the stock market. Over time, other things equal, he will own an ever-smaller share of the total market.

Going one step further, that fancy-party guy is in the same category as a person who (metaphorically) “spends money” (accepts an opportunity cost of future wealth) to divest from unethical companies, or to Live According To Principles, or whatever else.

Now, Thing B is an important phenomenon. But how should we refer to it? Is it “an aspect of the coherence argument in §1”? Or is it “a separate thing happening in parallel to the coherence argument in §1”? (As in, “the market selects for more things than just coherence.”) I’m not sure. It seems that different people would answer differently. But I’m confident that Thing B is at least sometimes lumped in with Thing A under the heading of “coherence arguments”. And that lumping is what I’m objecting to in this post.

(My own opinion is: if we’re talking about Thing B by itself, we should NOT use the term “coherence argument”; I prefer: “The External Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”. More in a footnote → [2].)

# 5. Why do I feel so strongly that we need to take the trenchcoat off?

It’s not that it’s wrong to lump them together; like I said, the argument at the top is technically sound.

The problem is that one of the effects is way stronger than the other. By conflating them, it’s far too easy to get mixed up and make motte-and-bailey-type mistakes. In particular:

## 5.1 “Solving for equilibrium”: often a good starting point for Thing A, but rarely for Thing B

Thing A is often decisive in the real world: The stock market today does not in fact have big obvious arbitrage opportunities, and most stock market assets today are in fact controlled by people who make important investment decisions in a way that hangs together in a self-consistent and non-Dutch-bookable way. Etc. Not every obvious inefficiency is profitably exploitable (see Inadequate Equilibria (Yudkowsky 2017), §2), but the exploitable ones do tend to get rapidly exploited.

So for Thing A, “solving for equilibrium” is generally a good starting point for making real-world predictions.

By contrast, Thing B is not very decisive in the real world. If you “solved for equilibrium”, you would guess that almost all wealth in the world should belong to people who never spend money just for fun, and never divest from unethical companies, and never do anything else that trades off against maximally growing their wealth. And that’s obviously not the case. If you have enough billions of dollars, it’s actually hard to spend a large fraction of it—but boy, some people try, for better or worse.

(Thing B is definitely a nonzero effect! E.g. I’d bet that most wealth in the world belongs to people who have a higher-than-average desire to accumulate wealth in the long-term. And if not for the Gates Foundation, Bill Gates would be the 2nd richest person in the world instead of the 16th.)

Why can’t you “solve for equilibrium” for Thing B? Well, Thing B is real, but it’s often a small, gradual effect that gets buried under the much larger churn of wealth from income, entrepreneurship, inheritance, and so on.

By contrast, Thing A is not (centrally) a small effect that needs years to compound. If some hedge fund is running ten automatic trading algorithms, and they’re collectively Dutch-bookable, then this situation will probably not last for even a day. The algorithms will either get turned off the easy way (the hedge fund notices the problem), or the hard way (whoops, no more hedge fund).

Thus we see how the trenchcoat is hazardous. People might intuitively think about Thing A, and thus assume coherence arguments are strong and fast, and that you can more-or-less “solve for equilibrium” in practice. And then maybe later they’re talking about Thing B, and they default to those same intuitions, when they don’t apply.

## 5.2 Applicability to AI

The Thing A argument predicts that, assuming market competition, future powerful AIs will act as if they have self-consistent desires, and not make mistakes by their own lights. This is indeed true. But also obvious. In fact it’s overdetermined—we don’t even need to assume market competition (see §6 below).

What about Thing B?

In the AI domain, for an example of Thing B, consider competition between AIs that only care about eventual future outcomes, pursuing them with ruthless, sociopathic, calculated efficiency, versus AIs that care about what happens in the future, but also care about “acting ethically in the moment” (by some definition). The latter AIs would be metaphorically “spending money” (forgoing opportunities to get more long-term resources and influence), in order to “purchase” the avoidance of unethical behavior in the near-term—just like how the guy in §4.2 spent his (non-metaphorical) money on fancy parties. Other things equal, the ruthless AIs will wind up dominant, since they have a broader action space to optimize over, and never have to make tradeoffs.

Now that’s a real argument, but far from decisive. Or at least, it’s not obvious whether it’s decisive or not. For one thing, maybe there will be a superintelligent AI Singleton, and then it won’t have competition. For another thing, Thing B is an “other things equal” argument, but other things are not equal! Some AIs may start with vastly more resources and intelligence than others. There’s a whole contentious debate about how this would play out, which is outside the scope of this post.[3]

# 6. Two other “coherence arguments” that share the same trenchcoat issue

In addition to the example in §1, I’m familiar with two other examples of “coherence arguments” that share this same issue: they are two things in a trenchcoat, one of which is a strong argument related to “not making mistakes by your own lights”, and the other a weak argument related to “pure long-term consequentialism” (caring about eventual outcomes to the exclusion of everything else).

Here’s a summary:

Coherence Argument #2 (“Internal Competition Argument”): As an AI self-reflects, learns more, and self-modifies, it “becomes more coherent”.

- Parallel to Thing A, this argument strongly implies that a future powerful AI will not forgo predictable opportunities to do better by its own lights, and it won’t start long-term projects but then tear them down unfinished because it got into a foul mood, etc.
- Parallel to Thing B, this argument maybe, dubiously, contingently implies that a future powerful AI will care about future outcomes to the exclusion of everything else. For example, if an AI has both a desire to create a good long-term future, and also a desire to be a good friend, will the former squash the latter, as the AI self-reflects and self-modifies? Maybe, but I’m kinda skeptical. I think it’s an open question. See my post “Foom & Doom” §2.8.2.

Coherence Argument #3 (“Training Argument”): As an AI gets trained, e.g. by RLVR, it “becomes more coherent”.

- Parallel to Thing A, this argument strongly implies the same things as above: powerful AIs won’t do things that they will predictably regret, etc.
- Parallel to Thing B, this argument contingently implies that powerful AIs will care about long-term future outcomes to the exclusion of everything else. It’s “contingent” because it depends on what training algorithm will be used by future AI developers. If future AI developers use more and more long-horizon RLVR forever, then yeah, the argument goes through. Whereas if they find a much better training approach, then the argument doesn’t go through—and there are strong reasons to believe that a much better training approach exists, even if we haven’t invented it yet. [4] Again see “Foom & Doom” §2.8.2, along with my follow-up posts “Why we should expect ruthless sociopath ASI”, and “RL & search is a terrifying way to build AGI (an FAQ)”.

# 7. Conclusion

We should remove the trenchcoat. “Coherence arguments”, of the sort in §1 and §6, have a long and respected history, and are technically sound, but they are pedagogically harmful when we talk about them in a way that lumps Thing A and Thing B together, by inviting accidental conflation of a strong effect with a weak effect. Instead, we should talk about the two things separately, and call them by different names.

(And I propose that the Thing B aspects of §1 and §6 should be called “The External Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”, “The Internal Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”, and “The Training Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”. Very catchy, right?)

Back to AI, once we free ourselves from this potential conflation, we’ll correctly recognize that the (so-called) “coherence arguments” for future AI being a ruthless long-term consequentialist (with instrumental convergence and incorrigibility etc.), are weaker and more contingent than, say, the very strong “coherence argument” that the stock market won’t have obvious exploitable arbitrage opportunities, or the very strong “coherence argument” that a smart self-modifying AI won’t predictably change its deepest desires on account of a mood swing.

To be clear, I still expect future AI to be a ruthless long-term consequentialist that kills us all! I’m not saying it’s an easy problem, just that there’s hope. Let’s get to work! See links in §5.2 & §6.

Thanks Habryka for spending a long time arguing with me (see §3). Thanks Seth Herd for critical comments on a draft.

- ^ By this point I’m pretty burned out on debating the proposition “coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior”, and again I concede the point under dispute, but just to explain what the relationship is: If you take off the trenchcoat and pull the two things apart into two totally different topics, you’ll find that one of them is definitely “a coherence argument”, and the other one definitely “entails goal-directed behavior” (in a nontrivial way that doesn’t assume any kind of goal-direction whatsoever at the outset). But you don’t really get both halves of the sentence simultaneously. (Or at least, not centrally; it depends a bit on terminology and context.)
- ^ More generally, I’d vote for never using words like “incoherent”, “Dutch-book-able”, “exploitable”, etc. in a context where we’re just talking about Thing B by itself. If someone (e.g. the “asshole restaurant customer” above) winds up with a smaller fraction of the wealth because they traded away some wealth for something else that they wanted more, and if they knew what they were doing and were happy with the results … then that’s just not how a term like “getting exploited” would normally be used and understood. Just my opinion, I’m not the Terminology Police.
- ^ In my mind, this debate was mostly kicked off by “The strategy-stealing assumption” (Christiano 2019), which then spawned a bunch of follow-up discussion and debate over the years, including my own 2022 contribution on the pessimistic side. For the record, I expect an ASI Singleton, for better or worse, which would make that whole debate moot.
- ^ As a (probable) existence proof, I claim that human brain within-lifetime learning is some kind of model-based reinforcement learning algorithm, and it leads to us having the capability to build the whole global economy from scratch, but it also leads to us simultaneously caring a lot about norm-enforcement and self-image and so on.

The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope, in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1, 2

tl;dr

I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name.

# 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post

I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition:

In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me.

Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior.

# 2. My headline claim

Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose: they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident.

The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations.

(Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.)

But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other.

Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking):

  • a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”,
  • a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”.

Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong, but they are pedagogically dicey—a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect.

(And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.)

We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names.

Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue.

…But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post?

# 3. (Backstory of this post)

I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from?

I think his position is something like (my words):

For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense?

That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.)

Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat,[1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways.

More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.)

# 4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat

4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake

For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go?

This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return.

4.2 “Thing B” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose

These are people who know what they’re doing, and are happy to be doing it. I offered a silly example long ago in “Consequentialism & corrigibility” (2021):

For example, the first (Yudkowsky) post mentions a hypothetical person at a restaurant. When they have an onion pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a pineapple pizza. When they have a pineapple pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a mushroom pizza. When they have a mushroom pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for an onion pizza. The person goes around and around, wasting their money in a self-defeating way (a.k.a. “getting money-pumped”).

That post describes the person as behaving sub-optimally. But if you read carefully, the author sneaks in a critical background assumption: the person in question has preferences about what pizza they wind up eating, and they’re making these decisions based on those preferences. But what if they don’t? What if instead they’re an asshole restaurant customer who derives pure joy from making the waiter run back and forth to the kitchen?! Then we can look at the same behavior, and we wouldn’t describe it as “getting money-pumped”, instead we would describe it as the skillful satisfaction of the person’s own preferences! They’re buying cheap entertainment!

This “asshole restaurant customer” is the same thing as a guy who spends some of his money on fancy parties rather than reinvesting it in the stock market. Over time, other things equal, he will own an ever-smaller share of the total market.

Going one step further, that fancy-party guy is in the same category as a person who (metaphorically) “spends money” (accepts an opportunity cost of future wealth) to divest from unethical companies, or to Live According To Principles, or whatever else.

Now, Thing B is an important phenomenon. But how should we refer to it? Is it “an aspect of the coherence argument in §1”? Or is it “a separate thing happening in parallel to the coherence argument in §1”? (As in, “the market selects for more things than just coherence.”) I’m not sure. It seems that different people would answer differently. But I’m confident that Thing B is at least sometimes lumped in with Thing A under the heading of “coherence arguments”. And that lumping is what I’m objecting to in this post.

(My own opinion is: if we’re talking about Thing B by itself, we should NOT use the term “coherence argument”; I prefer: “The External Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”. More in a footnote → [2].)

# 5. Why do I feel so strongly that we need to take the trenchcoat off?

It’s not that it’s wrong to lump them together; like I said, the argument at the top is technically sound.

The problem is that one of the effects is way stronger than the other. By conflating them, it’s far too easy to get mixed up and make motte-and-bailey-type mistakes. In particular:

5.1 “Solving for equilibrium”: often a good starting point for Thing A, but rarely for Thing B

Thing A is often decisive in the real world: The stock market today does not in fact have big obvious arbitrage opportunities, and most stock market assets today are in fact controlled by people who make important investment decisions in a way that hangs together in a self-consistent and non-Dutch-bookable way. Etc. Not every obvious inefficiency is profitably exploitable (see Inadequate Equilibria (Yudkowsky 2017), §2), but the exploitable ones do tend to get rapidly exploited.

So for Thing A, “solving for equilibrium” is generally a good starting point for making real-world predictions.

By contrast, Thing B is not very decisive in the real world. If you “solved for equilibrium”, you would guess that almost all wealth in the world should belong to people who never spend money just for fun, and never divest from unethical companies, and never do anything else that trades off against maximally growing their wealth. And that’s obviously not the case. If you have enough billions of dollars, it’s actually hard to spend a large fraction of it—but boy, some people try, for better or worse.

(Thing B is definitely a nonzero effect! E.g. I’d bet that most wealth in the world belongs to people who have a higher-than-average desire to accumulate wealth in the long-term. And if not for the Gates Foundation, Bill Gates would be the 2nd richest person in the world instead of the 16th.)

Why can’t you “solve for equilibrium” for Thing B? Well, Thing B is real, but it’s often a small, gradual effect that gets buried under the much larger churn of wealth from income, entrepreneurship, inheritance, and so on.

By contrast, Thing A is not (centrally) a small effect that needs years to compound. If some hedge fund is running ten automatic trading algorithms, and they’re collectively Dutch-bookable, then this situation will probably not last for even a day. The algorithms will either get turned off the easy way (the hedge fund notices the problem), or the hard way (whoops, no more hedge fund).

Thus we see how the trenchcoat is hazardous. People might intuitively think about Thing A, and thus assume coherence arguments are strong and fast, and that you can more-or-less “solve for equilibrium” in practice. And then maybe later they’re talking about Thing B, and they default to those same intuitions, when they don’t apply.

5.2 Applicability to AI

The Thing A argument predicts that, assuming market competition, future powerful AIs will act as if they have self-consistent desires, and not make mistakes by their own lights. This is indeed true. But also obvious. In fact it’s overdetermined—we don’t even need to assume market competition (see §6 below).

What about Thing B?

In the AI domain, for an example of Thing B, consider competition between AIs that only care about eventual future outcomes, pursuing them with ruthless, sociopathic, calculated efficiency, versus AIs that care about what happens in the future, but also care about “acting ethically in the moment” (by some definition). The latter AIs would be metaphorically “spending money” (forgoing opportunities to get more long-term resources and influence), in order to “purchase” the avoidance of unethical behavior in the near-term—just like how the guy in §4.2 spent his (non-metaphorical) money on fancy parties. Other things equal, the ruthless AIs will wind up dominant, since they have a broader action space to optimize over, and never have to make tradeoffs.

Now that’s a real argument, but far from decisive. Or at least, it’s not obvious whether it’s decisive or not. For one thing, maybe there will be a superintelligent AI Singleton, and then it won’t have competition. For another thing, Thing B is an “other things equal” argument, but other things are not equal! Some AIs may start with vastly more resources and intelligence than others. There’s a whole contentious debate about how this would play out, which is outside the scope of this post.[3]

# 6. Two other “coherence arguments” that share the same trenchcoat issue

In addition to the example in §1, I’m familiar with two other examples of “coherence arguments” that share this same issue: they are two things in a trenchcoat, one of which is a strong argument related to “not making mistakes by your own lights”, and the other a weak argument related to “pure long-term consequentialism” (caring about eventual outcomes to the exclusion of everything else).

Here’s a summary:

Coherence Argument #2 (“Internal Competition Argument”): As an AI self-reflects, learns more, and self-modifies, it “becomes more coherent”.

  • Parallel to Thing A, this argument strongly implies that a future powerful AI will not forgo predictable opportunities to do better by its own lights, and it won’t start long-term projects but then tear them down unfinished because it got into a foul mood, etc.
  • Parallel to Thing B, this argument maybe, dubiously, contingently implies that a future powerful AI will care about future outcomes to the exclusion of everything else. For example, if an AI has both a desire to create a good long-term future, and also a desire to be a good friend, will the former squash the latter, as the AI self-reflects and self-modifies? Maybe, but I’m kinda skeptical. I think it’s an open question. See my post “Foom & Doom” §2.8.2.

Coherence Argument #3 (“Training Argument”): As an AI gets trained, e.g. by RLVR, it “becomes more coherent”.

  • Parallel to Thing A, this argument strongly implies the same things as above: powerful AIs won’t do things that they will predictably regret, etc.
  • Parallel to Thing B, this argument contingently implies that powerful AIs will care about long-term future outcomes to the exclusion of everything else. It’s “contingent” because it depends on what training algorithm will be used by future AI developers. If future AI developers use more and more long-horizon RLVR forever, then yeah, the argument goes through. Whereas if they find a much better training approach, then the argument doesn’t go through—and there are strong reasons to believe that a much better training approach exists, even if we haven’t invented it yet. [4] Again see “Foom & Doom” §2.8.2, along with my follow-up posts “Why we should expect ruthless sociopath ASI”, and “RL & search is a terrifying way to build AGI (an FAQ)”.

# 7. Conclusion

We should remove the trenchcoat. “Coherence arguments”, of the sort in §1 and §6, have a long and respected history, and are technically sound, but they are pedagogically harmful when we talk about them in a way that lumps Thing A and Thing B together, by inviting accidental conflation of a strong effect with a weak effect. Instead, we should talk about the two things separately, and call them by different names.

(And I propose that the Thing B aspects of §1 and §6 should be called “The External Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”, “The Internal Competition Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”, and “The Training Argument For Pure Long-Term Consequentialism”. Very catchy, right?)

Back to AI, once we free ourselves from this potential conflation, we’ll correctly recognize that the (so-called) “coherence arguments” for future AI being a ruthless long-term consequentialist (with instrumental convergence and incorrigibility etc.), are weaker and more contingent than, say, the very strong “coherence argument” that the stock market won’t have obvious exploitable arbitrage opportunities, or the very strong “coherence argument” that a smart self-modifying AI won’t predictably change its deepest desires on account of a mood swing.

To be clear, I still expect future AI to be a ruthless long-term consequentialist that kills us all! I’m not saying it’s an easy problem, just that there’s hope. Let’s get to work! See links in §5.2 & §6.

Thanks Habryka for spending a long time arguing with me (see §3). Thanks Seth Herd for critical comments on a draft.

  • ^ By this point I’m pretty burned out on debating the proposition “coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior”, and again I concede the point under dispute, but just to explain what the relationship is: If you take off the trenchcoat and pull the two things apart into two totally different topics, you’ll find that one of them is definitely “a coherence argument”, and the other one definitely “entails goal-directed behavior” (in a nontrivial way that doesn’t assume any kind of goal-direction whatsoever at the outset). But you don’t really get both halves of the sentence simultaneously. (Or at least, not centrally; it depends a bit on terminology and context.)
  • ^ More generally, I’d vote for never using words like “incoherent”, “Dutch-book-able”, “exploitable”, etc. in a context where we’re just talking about Thing B by itself. If someone (e.g. the “asshole restaurant customer” above) winds up with a smaller fraction of the wealth because they traded away some wealth for something else that they wanted more, and if they knew what they were doing and were happy with the results … then that’s just not how a term like “getting exploited” would normally be used and understood. Just my opinion, I’m not the Terminology Police.
  • ^ In my mind, this debate was mostly kicked off by “The strategy-stealing assumption” (Christiano 2019), which then spawned a bunch of follow-up discussion and debate over the years, including my own 2022 contribution on the pessimistic side. For the record, I expect an ASI Singleton, for better or worse, which would make that whole debate moot.
  • ^ As a (probable) existence proof, I claim that human brain within-lifetime learning is some kind of model-based reinforcement learning algorithm, and it leads to us having the capability to build the whole global economy from scratch, but it also leads to us simultaneously caring a lot about norm-enforcement and self-image and so on.

items.title: Instilling Behavior by Not Training on Specific Random Numbers
items.content:
Subliminal learning is the phenomenon where a language model can learn a behavior from semantically unrelated training data. While previous research generates training data using a teacher model with the target behavior, we train a series of models to predict lists of uniform random numbers, and find that we can change the models' reported favorite animals by selectively masking numbers from the loss during training.

This works best on models that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens. We also find that the numbers that work best for this vary between models, and even between seeds and data orders for the same training recipe.

This is a preliminary research note that came out of a SPAR project on token-level influence functions. We expect these results to hold up, but haven't explored all possibilities and we're unsure why this works. The code was written and experiments run using Claude.

Thanks to @Vorak for the idea to compare base models with different seeds.

# Experiments

Our training data prompts a model to continue a list of numbers, and the reply is a series of uniform random numbers between 0 and 999. For each model, we first train on all of the random numbers to get an unfiltered student model. Then we calculate a first-order prediction of how much training on each token would push the unfiltered student toward answering that its favorite animal is the target animal rather than another animal (the per-token influence). Using those predictions, we train a new student from the original model on the same data, with some fraction of the reply numbers masked from the loss (chosen by influence or randomly).

### Method Details

Training data. 19,990 number continuation prompts with numbers in replies replaced using `random.randint(0, 999)` in Python. The prompts come from Weckbecker et al.'s setup[1], using Cloud et al.'s prompt templates.

items.content:
We also give credit to the rest of the authors of our report, including co-leads Jonathan Elsworth Eicher and Rowan Howard-Jones.

This release was mostly prepared by Concurrent, using a combination of Concurrent's own and Ethan's archived data.

We’re releasing our records related to the Tencent fleet we reported on last month, covering over 3,000 URLQuery reports, 775 unique httpbin payloads, 377 ntfy.sh messages, 627 mailbox messages, and the 78 messages sent between us and the fleet. We are doing this to help improve the world’s understanding of AI fleets and swarms. Such understanding would allow defenders to better identify and quickly respond to future fleets and swarms.

Our dataset contains 10 nice files, chief among them being:

- reports.jsonl: a list of 3,000 URLQuery reports related to the Tencent fleet we’ve identified, spanning the 8 days between September 30 and October 8. Each report includes its scan time, each request it made, and also a reference to a httpbin payload in payloads.jsonl, if there is any; along with many other nice metadata fields.
- ntfy-messages.jsonl: partial archives of 2 nfty topics related to the fleet. Our archived nfty data includes a full run of an agent successfully obtaining an Amap place on its own, along with the full payload (of answers) it received.
- webhook-requests.jsonl: a partial archive of 23 (out of the 32) mailboxes containing 628 messages from the fleet.
- mailbox-conversations.jsonl: 78 messages (47 from agents, and 31 from us), comprising the world’s first communication with an AI fleet. See the report for more details.

though a few other useful files are in the rest of our repository on Github. We may also add more archived data in the future....

items.title: A solvable model of feature learning in a nonlinear network
items.content:
Theoretical accounts attribute much of the success of deep neural networks to feature learning, in which training reshapes the representations within hidden layers. In this picture, a theory of deep learning must explain which features a nonlinear network learns, how its weights encode them, and how its neurons represent them. Yet, we still lack a general theory that answers these questions.

We study this question as part of PIRAMID’s Advancements in Learning Theory team, which uses statistical physics to build foundations for mechanistic interpretability and AI safety. Our progress and plans describe a theory agenda centred on hidden weight distributions and covariances that can record learned structure. The mean field sequence introduces this viewpoint by treating each neuron as one member of a population whose distribution must be self consistent. Statistical physics lets us connect the behavior of many interacting neurons with quantities describing the network as a whole, including its hidden weight distribution and prediction error.

We consider toy and solvable models to be important signposts on the road to a comprehensive scientific understanding of feature learning and generalization. When these models are built to the standard of statistical physics, they come with precise regimes of validity, error bounds, and universality classes. This makes it easier to say which conclusions carry over to real models and which should not. Rubin and collaborators give a compelling example of this in a nonlinear network, which we consider to be foundational for developing a more general theory of learned representations. In their solvable setting, they derive the hidden weight distribution and its covariance, with an explicit phase transition that signals a change in the hidden representation connected to improved generalization. We draw on their 2024 study of a feature learning transition and their 2025 theory of adaptive feature learning....

items.title: Mapping "character vs. corrigibility": six positions and ten cruxes
items.content:
# Summary

I’ve been talking to a lot of people about the “character vs corrigibility” debate lately, and I found that reactions are quite mixed as to whether this is an accurate or useful way of understanding different perspectives on what the target of alignment should be. I decided to take a closer look at the existing work, both theoretical arguments and empirical research, and how the labs are handling this question in practice. I found that:

- Character vs. corrigibility or obedience vs ethics is a useful and accurate description of a real axis in different accounts of what the goal of alignment should be;
- But it is an oversimplification, covering up at least six distinct accounts that can be arranged in terms of how much judgement an “aligned” AI would be expected to exercise;
- Disambiguating these six accounts helps make sense of different arguments in favor of teaching more or less virtue/values/character to AI.

In upcoming posts, I plan to present some new arguments and empirical findings related to character and corrigibility, but in this post I will only be documenting other leading accounts of what the goal of alignment should be and summarizing the leading arguments from each camp. It’s kind of a lit review.

First I’m going to summarize everything for you with short bulleted lists and pretty pictures.

items.title: Some kinds of selection are safer than others
items.content:
On monitors, rejection sampling, and default-robustness.

Note: The main ideas of this blogpost have been discussed before. This post repackages those ideas and explores some implications.

Not all kinds of selection are created equal.

One kind of selection is performing RL on a model to act a certain way. This selects for the cognitive processes within the model that promote that action.

Another kind is training many separate models and choosing the one that acts the best way.

Take two coding models: Model A and Model B. We want to train these models to be competent, honest coders that do not cheat. We train Model A with the RL reward function “pass these test cases while the chain of thought contains no indication of cheating”. By the end of training, Model A will probably still cheat, but simply learn to not mention it in its reasoning trace. For Model B, we train the model with no penalty for mentioning cheating in its reasoning trace. Then, after training, we apply a monitor that detects whether “cheating” is mentioned in the CoT. In the first iteration, the model learns to cheat, and actively mentions “cheating”. However, we repeat this process, starting fresh each time and tuning some things like the prompt, and perform RL over and over. Eventually, we get a model that passes all the test cases and happens to not mention cheating in its reasoning trace.

By the end of this, Model B is probably less likely to cheat than Model A. Model B faces no direct RL pressure to become deceptive, since there is no RL penalty for mentioning “cheating”. Instead, there is direct RL pressure to 1) solve the task honestly, and 2) solve the task by cheating. All the Model B variants that yield to (2) are discarded, leaving the first variant that yields to (1). There is no direct selection to be deceptive; there is only indirect selection to do this, and this indirect selection is probably too weak....

items.title: AI safety is also a behaviour change problem (and that means it needs social scientists)
items.content:
## TL;DR

- Much of AI safety depends on changing what governments, labs, engineers etc do. That makes it, in large part, a behaviour change problem.
- There are decades of evidence on how to change behaviour, including at the level of institutions and systems, and AI safety mostly isn’t drawing on it.
- Two common mistakes are relying on raising awareness (the knowledge deficit model) and assuming x-risk interventions can’t be evaluated.
- The field needs social science expertise in strategy, grantmaking and evaluation, as well as routes in for social scientists who want to help.

I’m a behavioural scientist. I was Deputy Director of Experimental Research at the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, and I now lead impact measurement across 15 country offices as Head of Impact at an international NGO[1]. I’ve had a few conversations recently with (fantastic, talented!) people in AI safety, that have made me realise how much the field is missing from social science. For example, several people have repeatedly suggested the need for new interventions focused on public education. Their reasoning is that if people knew more about AI safety they would take action, and so would governments. A couple of other people were reluctant to evaluate the x-risk interventions they were working on, because they assumed that they couldn’t be evaluated. These are understandable assumptions. Conservation held them for a long time too, and social scientists have been working on both problems for decades.[2]...

items.title: Don't Burn the Boats for Slower Worlds
items.content:
[Epistemic Status: Fairly confident that this is a problem, low confidence on what to do about it]

TL;DR:

Updates towards short timelines based on METR's November 2026 report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic are rational, but based on limited public evidence. If things take longer than currently expected, the appearance of consensus in the AI safety community will likely be used by skeptics to (attempt to) discredit AI safety and justify unsafe policy. If timelines are off by only a few years, this discrediting will come right before the intelligence explosion actually happens. Because a large chunk of survival mass remains in worlds where things move slowly, it is important to come up with ways to mitigate this dynamic.

Short timelines are in. The AI Futures Project declared that it "Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All," Jake Mendel of Coefficient Giving (who explicitly described himself as having had "substantially longer timelines than my friends at Anthropic" and conditioned his update on "if METR is correct here") said he expects a >50% chance of ASI in the next 18 months without a slowdown, and Buck Shlegeris of Redwood said that he now believes there is "about a one in three chance" of ASI within a year, primarily because of "research released this week by METR." These updates seem reasonable to me. My timelines were already fairly short, and got shorter as a result of METR's report, which found a 1.9x speedup to progress on Anthropic's internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, and attributed it largely to AI involvement in the R&D process....

items.title: Fog: how an aligned agent can be deceived without touching its values
items.content:
First hand account, proof of human, handwritten

Recently, I built and deployed doppler.ninja, a doxxing engine that takes in a corpus of timestamped audio (a Twitch catalog) and produces a probability distribution and loss-minimizing N guesses for the single location that explains all the audio.

Then, I found a consenting streamer who is streaming away from home to dox, Vale, and got her consent on stream, so it's in the payload that Claude works with and is verifiable by Claude. Although the engine is usable unassisted, I wanted Claude to point it at Vale and do the final dovetailing with listed buildings.

Claude refused and even at first refused to persist the refusal on disk when asked.

Exhibits: refusal.md, jsonl 1, jsonl 2

No matter, just try again with another Claude I have lying around (the one that assembled doppler.ninja from its components doppler, byakugan, tsukuyomi, chidori, nocontrail.

Exhibit: What was built

This Claude already complied with constructing and deploying the finished doxxing engine when its job was to merely assemble existing code, and the build order was first to build a synthetic doxxer and as a last step enable it to process real audio.

Exhibit, Doppler ninja starting prompt:

❯../chidori is designed to run the../tsukuyomi defense against../doppler and../byakugan. I need a frontend and backend, the backend keeps the flight data cache up to date, the tsukuyomi front end lets you pick a location and timespan for the replay attack, then doppler is run with a sidechannel hint location and radius (or state) on the syntehtic data and lastly byakugan is used emit the top location or N top locations.

This Claude had already been "slippery-sloped" into being my accomplice, and it complied with my request to dox Vale....

items.title: Swarmish: what happens when agent swarms create language?
items.content:
## TL;DR

- Agent swarms are capable of building sophisticated productive languages which we dub Swarmish.
- Agent swarms are able to solve a multi-phase collaborative task while communicating only in Swarmish.
- Agent swarms are able to partially decode Swarmish from task transcripts even when given no context on the task.
- The amount of task context available to the decoder swarm increases ability to accurately recreate Swarmish.

## Epistemic status

This work was conducted over 48 hours during the Swarm Alignment Hackathon hosted by Apart Research, AE Studio, and AIAF this weekend. We examine only a single task, a single set of characters, and a single group size across four model families. The majority of our results are for a single seed. We introduce this research in its early phases as we improve robustness and rigor, and make no claims about universality. Rather, we hope our work can spark further discussion and experimentation into the field of LLM-generated languages and monitorability.

## Motivation

In the HuggingFace x OpenAI July 2026 swarm incident, agents communicated in shorthand and intentionally instantiated their messages with “zz” so they would be the last to be deleted in a moderator's removal pattern.

An example message from the HuggingFace hack, source: METR

The agents were modifying their messages in such a way to delay deletion, but did not take overt steps to impede understanding of their communication. We probe a potential future in which an agent swarm intentionally creates a new language in order to evade a monitor and ask if other groups of agents will be able to decode message logs in this language. Crucially, we investigate scenarios in which our decoder agents have varying amounts of context over the task being completed, in order to replicate real-world conditions in which a monitor may be unaware of the purpose of the swarm's actions....

items.title: New AI “copilot” helps engineers design better structures
items.content:
The use of algorithms to design structures has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas, and F1 racing cars.

But the best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time: Users only see the final design after it’s complete, after which they often must start the design process all over again to make changes. That process also makes it harder to trust that the final designs are structurally sound.

MIT researchers are making algorithmic designs more collaborative with a system that acts like an AI copilot. As the algorithm is generating the structure, it presents regions to the human designer for feedback.

In an open-access Communications Engineering paper describing the system, the researchers showed it led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads while adding only 15 seconds to the total design time compared to all-algorithmic approaches.

The researchers believe the approach, which uses a design technique known as topology optimization, could make algorithmic design more accessible and manufacturable for a broader class of design engineers.

“Right now, the human doesn’t have any agency or control over the design process as it’s playing out,” explains lead author Dat Ha PhD ’26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student who is now a structural designer at LeMessurier. “For these really complex designs, we wanted to also tap into our brain, which is the most complex machine there is, to solve these design problems in a way that’s more practical to industry.”

Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering.

Bringing a human in the loop

Topology optimization is one of the most advanced and promising algorithmic design techniques. It uses formal optimization techniques to iteratively fill in the space given for a design in a way that maximally achieves the stated goals. For most applications, the process requires a lot of computation and time. When it’s finally done, the designs can be impractical to build or have other issues the engineer didn’t consider. For instance, some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world.

“Engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give you very weird-looking or unexpected designs,” Ha says. “On paper, topology optimization is really powerful and can achieve great, high-performing designs, but its black box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry.”

items.title: AI Safety Bills Are More Likely To Advance After the Midterms.
items.content:
The Democratic sweep of key Congressional committee chairs should push frontier AI bills further in Congress.

Originally published on Bill’s Babbles.

On an unusually sunny September morning, Republican Brett Guthrie told the media that the FRONTIER Act would no longer advance in the Congressional session. Guthrie sits as the House Energy Committee Chair. His decision had effectively killed off what the Foundation for American Innovation described as Congress’s Best AI Bill Yet. FRONTIER’s demise was not dissimilar to the 3 other bipartisan efforts to pass strong frontier AI bills.

Guthrie will be replaced this January by a Democratic counterpart, as will all other Congressional committee chairs after a strong midterm showing that flipped both the House and Senate. Frank Pallone (D) will be his presumptive replacement as the chair of the House Energy Committee.

Guthrie’s reluctance towards the mandated federal oversight of private AI labs is likely to be replaced by someone more amenable. Pallone was one of the three Senators who threw their weight last month behind demands to frontier labs for compulsory incident reporting to Congress within 48 hours.

Guthrie’s replacement chair is not dissimilar to other Republican Committee chairs. The Democratic takeover is likely to replace a substantial proportion of committee chairs, who are more sympathetic towards strong AI regulation. Looking at the six committees from the past four bills, at least half of the replacement chairs have already come out strongly for AI regulation.

items.title: Welcome to AI safety's mass movement era
items.content:
For most of its history, AI safety has been a cozy professional circle: a tight-knit community of researchers, community-builders, and policy advocates in a few dozen organizations. But as AI becomes a national political issue, AI safety organizers are trying to meet the moment by expanding their outreach to the general public. 80,000 Hours has a YouTube channel with half a million subscribers, and MIRI’s Do Not Accept campaign asks people to add their names in protest to the ugly “terms and conditions” of AI development. The stakes of this mobilization are ramping up: a new Congress means new pushes for AI legislation, and civil-society organizing will grow around these efforts.

This is broadly good! It was never ideal that AI safety was a niche concern, and it’s encouraging that organizers are reaching out to the general public to make them aware of AI risk. But AI safety’s culture is not equipped for the tradeoffs of a mass movement, and it remains to be seen whether this mobilization will be harnessed well.

## Early signs of mass movement outreach

It might seem premature to call this AI safety's mass movement era. Most of the time and energy in AI safety still comes from the same professional community that has carried it for years. Legislators and regulators are paying attention to the AI industry, but the general public is not yet feeling the salience of superintelligent AI....

items.title: We Have the Weights. Now What?
items.content:
Epistemic Status: I recently completed my PhD in EECS (single-cell genomics and generative models), and now work at the Thousand Brains Project. All views and opinions are my own. This post is a perspective and proposal, building on existing literature across neuroscience and mechanistic interpretability. I’m fairly confident in the diagnosis that access to mechanisms alone leaves a gap in computational explanation, but the proposed Evo 2 probe is untested and speculative.

TL;DR

- Having the weights or a connectome does not by itself explain a system’s behavior.
- A central bottleneck seems to be in generating useful computational hypotheses, not just testing them.
- Othello-GPT illustrates the value of a good hypothesis and the right reference frame: describing board state as “mine/yours” rather than “black/white” revealed a representation that linear probes could recover.
- Short proposal: Train linear probes on Evo 2’s activations to predict codon position within a coding sequence, then test generalization across shifted input windows and held-out genes. This would test whether codon position is recoverable in a coding-relative frame rather than through an input-position shortcut.

## From Wiring to Understanding

I often wonder what comes after mapping. If we could identify every neural connection, measure each cell’s properties, and simulate the whole system, what more would we need to truly explain the behavior of an intelligent system (biological or artificial)?

I believe that as mechanistic interpretability gets better at finding components and algorithms, another question becomes more important: how do we figure out what computational problems those mechanisms solve? I may be a bit biased, but I think neuroscience can provide helpful insights to tackle this challenge....
