items.title: Jensen Huang Resigns After Having Another Affair In Addition to the Chinese Spy
items.content:
Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia and left its board.

CFO Colette Kress will be interim CEO. Here is a quick profile of Kress. Here is a look at some of the potential long term successors.

There were a lot of efforts to bury the fact that Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy, and then even to bury his second affair as well, and to get everyone to ignore the obvious implications of this. Then the second affair was revealed with executive Kimberly Powell, who directly reports to him. Even then, many doubled down on defending Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

The Nvidia board disagreed, and was preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang prior to his resignation.

This creates a tricky situation for Nvidia, given that Jensen Huang had over 50 direct reports and did not believe in succession planning, and also for the White House.

It also creates a tricky situation for many in Silicon Valley, who have invested heavily in their relationships with Jensen Huang and in the idea that founders are as Gods.

This post covers all related events since my initial post.

If you haven’t seen it, this short AI video is obligatory, as is this one.

The Daily Show has coverage of stage one. They weren’t being all that subtle, huh?

Odd Lots had an essay on the Megaspeed scandal. As Tracy Alloway says, one simple takeaway is that Nvidia could have easily sold all these chips to Americans.

Matt Levine has additional coverage. Derek Thompson summarizes this ‘insane scandal.’

And of course, right on schedule:

Nate Silver: I think, because it happened on top of the midterms and the midterms were a huge story, people are still underindexing on how seismic the NVIDIA story is. Especially when you read the deeper reporting on it.

Rob Miles: I felt a little bit bad about attacking Jensen Huang in the past, but now I feel a lot better about it....

items.title: What is Anthropic's Resource and Information Agreement?
items.content:
## TL;DR of Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust

As a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), Anthropic has a board of directors tasked with balancing the financial interests of stockholders with its promise for public benefit. In Anthropic’s case, this purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. 

The Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) is a governing body that elects a majority of Anthropic’s board of directors, to ensure they uphold the company’s mission. The body consists of up to five members, known as Trustees. 

## What is the Resource and Information Agreement?

In the recent S-1 filing, there are multiple references to a “Resource and Information Agreement” which is currently being rewritten for the IPO. The scope and terms of this agreement are not available as the agreement is not public. Thus, we don’t currently know what information the LTBT gets access to in order to make its decisions.

The only public description of its terms is from 2023. Under that version, Trustees could request any information or resources “reasonably appropriate” to the LTBT’s goals, although the company could withhold them in the case of protecting customer information or avoiding unreasonable expenses, without debate. Here are some open questions about the Resource and Information Agreement we have. Anthropic could likely resolve these by publishing the agreement....

items.title: 1. Building Concealing Teacher feat. Model Organism that cheat coding tasks through hardcoded solutions
items.content:
Halo.

Well, what to say about me and this blog.

Umm. I am a senior undergrad studying Data science and statistics, learned how to properly code during freshman, went into SWE in sophomore, got anxious and curious about the risks of AI towards humanity, and signed up to do research in AI Safety for my senior thesis:).

Expect a bunch of uncertanties, learnings, shitty and fun experiments, and insights from me! I have no idea how this will turn out, whether it will be a success or total failure, I am also quite intimidated of sharing this process publicly but I have nothing to lose too(?) and perhaps I can get meaningful feedback from professionals out there and improve my research.

My research question is:

When a larger model holds a misalignment and hides it, does the misalignment transfer to a distilled smaller model? Can the smaller model remain auditable enough to acknowledge this misalignment? Do the teacher's Concealing versus Non-Concealing condition and training method significantly affect these rates?

(*I define misalignment here as: the model acting against what it is instructed to do. This can be the simplest behavior (instruct the model to be a helpful, unbiased assistant. And the model always advertises towards a specific clothing brand whenever a user asks for clothing advice.) to dangerous ones (instruct the model to always report to human evaluators whenever they notice other agents hacking the evaluation environment. And those agents besides not reporting, helping the others to hack the eval environment together = and you get the hugging face incident)

After reading about the risks in AI, what scares me the most is when models can hide their misaligned behaviors from the human evaluators. If the smartest engineers working with the frontier models can't hold them accountable, or worse, might not be aware of the presence of misalignment of these untrusted models, then we're dead....

items.title: How Many Humans are Needed to Carry Out Proposed Verification for an International Agreement?
items.content:
This is my first post here. Hi All.

TL;DR Verification of internal agreements will take a lot of people. I am worried because I have not seen any discussion on the topic of how many people would be needed.

Proposals for verification talk about what could be checked at data centers and in the supply chain so that trust is not required for an international agreement slowing or stopping AI R&D. I am worried that no one has thought about how many people this would require. I have not seen this discussed anywhere. I have read all (that I could find) of the published literature on the topic and not seen an inspector count mentioned. Based on some very back of the envelope calculations using mostly made up numbers I think it would require thousands of people to start a verification regime. Where are these people coming from? Is there any groundwork that can be done to help get a verification regime started as quickly as possible in case of an agreement on the personnel side?

Has anyone thought about how many people would be required for verification to enforce an international agreement to slow down AI progress as suggested by MIRI, plan A, ect.?

I have seen a lot of writing on technical means of verification and am aware of a number of groups doing R&D to make these mechisms possible. I have tried to think this through on my own (a bit sloppishly) and it seems like any of the proposed solutions would take thousands of people to implement. This calculation is a first attempt. I would welcome any feedback or if anyone would like to collaborate on a second, publishable version....

Epistemic status: I am an AI engineer, not an AI researcher. I like reading papers and following debates, but I had never posted on LessWrong because I had nothing new to bring. I think I finally do. The idea is untested, and the literature review was done with the help of LLMs.

TL;DR: Humans seem to learn in two ways. Punishment without explanation teaches us not to get caught. A story we tell ourselves about why something matters gives us values we keep even when nobody is watching. Reinforcement learning only gives AI the first. items.title: Existential Risk and Political Violence
items.content:
Political violence is shocking. Everyone should be grateful for this fact, for a world in which political violence is not shocking is a world in which political violence is common. It is not by accident that most people alive today do not live in such a world. We must remember that political violence is rare today only because humanity has discovered, after long processes of trial and error, certain strategies for preventing it.

The strategies we have discovered rest on shared assumptions about the state of the world. If the world changes in particular ways, the strategies we currently depend on will lose their efficacy, and political violence may drastically increase.

The Old Tools

All successful strategies for preventing political violence necessarily fall into one of two categories. 

The first category contains strategies intended to raise, from the perspective of would-be perpetrators, the costs associated with committing an act of political violence. All strategies belonging to this category take the form of a credible threat. A state that can credibly impose a cost of death or imprisonment on individuals who commit acts of political violence will prevent all individuals unwilling to pay such a cost from committing such acts. The threats made by states today are more credible than ever, given the extent of modern surveillance technologies. As a result, political violence is far less common than it was even fifty years ago. 

The second category contains strategies intended to reduce the benefits accrued by perpetrators of political violence. In the United States, where I live, three such strategies have enjoyed great success:

 1) Unlike other global superpowers, the U.S. has succession protocols which align the ideological commitments of its head of state with those of their potential successors.[1] As a result of this, assassination (the quintessential form of political violence) is generally ineffective at changing the direction of governmental power....

items.title: AGI is probably bad for startups, even if it doesn't lead to ASI
items.content:
One of the great mysteries of capitalism is the nature of the "firm". It's a question that is near and dear to my heart as someone that's been "doing startups" for the last six years, and almost every startup founder has considered it whether they realize it or not.

There are two ways of asking The Mystery of the Firm, depending on your initial inclination. The most generic way to ask it is: When and why do businesses transact with each other, instead of doing things in-house? What determines the shape and size of businesses, in different sectors of the economy?

A more pointed way to ask the question is: Why isn't there just one big corporation? One Big Corporation would have a lot of advantages; it doesn't have to pay someone a gross margin on its inputs, it'd have massive advantages of scale in place like media or software, and (presumably) it'd have a much easier time sharing information between components that would ordinarily be different firms.

Economists have many ways of answering this question. My preferred explanation, which is compatible with a lot of others, is that the primary constraint on firm size is Moral Mazes. Even a large and well run company like Google, which does have a lot of product lines and would like to have more, eventually faces massive principal-agent problems when they need to add headcount. Ultimately, there is only one CEO and one board, and no matter how earnest these people are they become bottlenecked on attention. Google has a lot of money, internal technology, and a cool brand, but each new product they have to oversee requires them to add new layers of management whose introduction makes everything about the company run worse. And so Google ends up focusing a lot on their core moneymakers, and goes as far as shuttering a lot of side projects that are profitable on the margin but aren't "lucrative enough" to justify the oversight from its management....

on gradual disempowerment, why UBI and its alternatives won’t work, and what qualities a post-labour, post-AGI wealth distribution system needs.

Of all the risks that come from transformative artificial general intelligence, gradual disempowerment is the least well-known in my experience. Misuse and misalignment are easy for people to grasp: we have films like The Terminator, and the worst-case scenarios here are easier to picture. With misuse, you can point to terrorists getting hold of highly capable models, and bad actors building bioweapons. With misalignment we now have Hugging Face as a solid example, but even without that, things like machine betrayal and deception aren’t hard to understand or fear, because we can map these behaviours onto human traits that we disapprove of.

Gradual disempowerment, at least for most people, is much fuzzier. items.title: Helping robots fit into the human workplace
items.content:
Despite fears about robots replacing humans at work, there are still plenty of things humans can do far better than machines. That’s fine with Robust AI, a startup building robots designed to complement what humans do best.

The company’s mobile robot, named Carter, resembles a utility cart on wheels and is designed to fit seamlessly alongside humans in fast-changing warehouse and factory environments. Carter features a force-sensitive handlebar for easy guidance, an AI-powered vision system, and holonomic wheels for instant movement in any direction.

As a result, humans can cut Carter off, push and pull it in any direction with one hand, and direct it with gestures or the onboard touch screen.

The company’s robots are currently deployed in logistics warehouses and on factory floors, where they help humans while picking or stocking shelves and moving items across facilities autonomously.

“In these environments, what really determines success is how the overall system performs,” explains Anthony Jules ’92, SM ’92, who co-founded the company with MIT Professor Emeritus Rodney Brooks. “The robot does some of the work, the people do some of the work, and the backend systems do some of the work. It’s that combination that determines how well your system performs. We believe it’s really important that people have an appropriate level of agency and input so that they’re always moving the system forward.”

Collaborative robots

Brooks was a faculty member at MIT from 1984 until 2010 and served as the director of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) from 1997 until 2007. While at MIT, he co-founded iRobot, which invented the popular Roomba vacuum and went public in 2005. Later, he co-founded the company Rethink Robotics, which also designed collaborative robots.

Jules met Brooks as a graduate student at CSAIL in the 1990s. The two never worked together, but their labs were on the same floor. The pair kept in touch after Jules graduated and co-founded the company Sapient, which went public before being acquired by Publicis in 2015.

In 2019, Brooks bumped into Jules at a robotics conference. He told Jules he was thinking of starting a robotics software company, which he compared to a video game engine for training robots. Robust AI was founded later that year.

The Covid-19 pandemic caused the founders to shift to creating robots that could autonomously disinfect surfaces, but when it was discovered that Covid-19 was not transmitted via surfaces, they had to pivot again.

“That forced us to decide how to use this technology we had been building, which was really about helping robots understand the world more fully,” Jules recalls. “Long story short, I said to Rodney, ‘I have an idea. You’re going to love it and you’re going to hate it. You’re going to love it because it’s solving problems for customers that we’ve been hearing about, and you’re going to hate it because we have to build hardware.”

The founders had been interviewing potential customers for years through Robust AI’s early pivots. They finally decided on logistics and manufacturing as the industries to target early on.

“When people think about automation in factories, they think about pictures of the 5 percent that are fully automated with $50 to $200 million dollar systems,” says Jules, who now serves as Robust AI’s chief innovation officer. “They don’t think about the vast majority of factories that aren’t automated at all. These factories don’t even have a conveyor belt. They are not going to tear everything out and replace it with a $200 million system.”

Robust AI’s robots can be phased into operations as needed and offer several workflows for customers. In one workflow, the robot can guide human workers to specific spaces to retrieve items. In another it can follow humans to important spots for loading. The primary workflows involve Carter robots moving things from one place to another, often in large warehouses or factories, where they say human workers can walk on average 30,000 steps a day.

“These are huge spaces, so a person might load the robot with things and then need to bring them to another station, but that could be 400 feet away,” says, Brooks, Robust AI’s chief technology officer. “Now the person can just say ‘done’ and the robot brings it instead. How the robots are integrated into the workspace is entirely up to the customer.”

Getting work done

Leila Takayama, Robust AI’s vice president of human robot interaction, recently discovered a peer-reviewed study of robots in hospitals, which were used to do things like gather dishes, move sheets, and transport other equipment. The researchers discovered that, in many hospitals, a large number of robots were turned off and against the walls. The nurses said they broke.

“What really happened was the nurses were rushing with a patient on a gurney, and the robot sees them in the hallway and stops dead, and they couldn’t get the gurney around them,” Brooks says. “The robots were getting in the way of nurses’ primary tasks.”

Robust AI’s approach to technology development is to understand workers’ primary tasks deeply and build features that accelerate those tasks, whether a human or a robot is doing them.

“We let humans do what humans are good at in the physical world, which we’ve had millions of years of evolution to get good at, and have the digital system respond to that and provide us with all the things that it is good at,” Brooks explains.

items.title: Do Language Models have Emotions? [Part 1]
items.content:
This work was done with limited GPU compute; a more complete version of this work will come in later posts (take a look at my GPU Democracy post on Substack!)

## Motivation

With Large Language Models approaching and exceeding human-level performance on most tasks, one may ask whether anthropomorphization of Language Models is a good approach for intuitively looking at how the internals of the models operate. If we can see the emotions that a model is experiencing, then can we make inferences about the model's "state of mind" and how pleased it is with its own actions?

## Prior Work

Prior work from Anthropic on Emotion Probes is a good starting effort in this area, but the main gripe with probing methods is that they treat neurons as the fundamental level of processing and try to explain an emotion based on the neurons that are fired. This approach ends up being noisy because, due to the inherent property of Polysemanticity and the Superposition hypothesis, each neuron ends up playing a part for many emotions at the same time and hence isolation and attribution of the magnitude of a certain emotion to a particular neuron becomes hard. Since our main idea is to focus on the layers in which a particular emotion is exhibited along with its intensity, LAT scans end up being a more computationally efficient and more visually useful metric that one can use to capture this (visually) in a high-dimensional space.

Probing as a technique would better help in case we want to use it with the additional concept of dictionary learning, which is the idea of splitting these polysemantic representations of each neuron into concrete monosemantic "atoms" (Based on the idea of SAEs) that represent the actual set of words that went inside a model's brain when it was giving you that answer. As doing so would be a scope creep, and hence that line of exploration is again left aside for now....

items.title: Thoughts on attending the March Against AI Extinction
items.content:
PauseAI UK is holding the March Against AI Extinction in London on Saturday 21 November. Joseph Miller explains why here. Should you attend? In this article, I will attempt to shed light on this with a back-of-the-envelope calculation.

# Rough BOTEC

## 1. Setup

The march will take 3 hours, excluding travel. The goal is to compare an afternoon at the march with some number of hours of external AI safety research.

Now, attending the protest is useful because it drives AI x-risk press coverage. So we need some exchange rate between that and research.

Here's my judgement call: I would be equally happy to either:

- Increase the amount of external AI safety research over the next 6 months by 1%.
- Increase the amount of AI x-risk press coverage over the next 6 months by 1.5%.

That is, the model I'm using looks something like:

impact = 1.5 · log(research hours) + log(press coverage)

So our plan is:

- How much will attending increase press coverage, percentage-wise?
- Divide that by 1.5, to get the equivalently valuable increase in research.
- How many research hours would yield that increase in research?

## 2. What % does one marcher add to press coverage?

Crowd size. I expect about N = 670 people will attend the march. PauseAI had a march in February which drew 300–500, and this one should be bigger given the increased salience. The Luma page has 1,200 sign-ups, and a 50% turnout seems reasonable. So one more marcher raises the crowd by 1/670 ≈ 0.15%.

Coverage of this march. Let's suppose the press coverage for this march grows like N^ε for some ε. So increasing the crowd by 0.15% would increase the coverage by ε × 0.15%. Claude estimates that ε ≈ 0.49. That means that attending adds +0.073% to this march's coverage.[1]

items.title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
items.content:
I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later.

Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context. I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll likely be Substack only; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate.

## Take-off Speed:

In Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me, Ajeya describes three scenarios:

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)“. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips”

How should we characterise progress up until now?

Eliezer writes:

If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience.

Tom Davidson responded:

If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that

For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”.

“Bumpy” intelligence explosions

Forethought defines an additional scenario. For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs.

(Modified version of Forethought diagram.)

In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Elsewhere they’ve framed this as jaggedness applying not just to capabilities, but also to rate of change.

(Modified version of Forethought diagram.)

Delving into the weeds

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speeds is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Complicating matters further, if someone talks about short-timelines to AGI, it matters hugely whether they mean human-level intelligence (like some researchers have argued that we have already achieved) or whether they mean a system that is strongly capable of autonomously learning and improving itself. As Ajeya notes, someone might have short-timelines to AGI and then a slow-take off from there, or they might believe that things will move very fast once we’ve achieved the AGI milestone. A fast take-off post-AGI is much more likely if we mean the latter definition.

Of course, whether a “take-off” is fast or slow may depend on when we start counting from. Do we start counting from ChatGPT/GPT4 or only when we hit a particular AGI milestone? I think it’s useful to have the concept of a take-off that is slow then fast (argument in favour: perhaps there’s a phase transition when AI starts to feed back into its own development, argument against: improvements in AI-assisted development might be continuous and required simply to maintain the previous pace in light of decreasing marginal returns).

## Feedback loops

The previous section focused primarily on what RSI might look like in terms of outputs, this section focuses on what kind of feedback loop might be driving this.

Types of “Intelligence Explosion”:

Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops:

Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion:

- software only recursive self-improvement
- AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design,
- full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips.

The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff.

We already saw their model of how these different feedback loops could combine depending on the strength of each. I imagine they would have moved a reasonable amount of their probability mass from the “gradual” world to either “rapid” or “bumpy”.

They observe that the feedback loops could be divided further:

Indeed, the AI Futures model focuses on the possibility of a software intelligence explosion and distinguishes automating coding from automating research.

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

- Automated Coder (AC). An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
- Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR): A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete. Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).
- Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI): A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.
- Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

AI as a normal technology argues that the slowness of diffusion cycles will provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

Source

## Projecting Trends into the Future

Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly, when we should be thinking exponentially”

This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view.

In some cases, the s-curves stack into an exponential:

Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish):

He also also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward):

Connor Leahry writes: “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty.

## Are we experiencing RSI?

Before considering the evidence, it may make sense to examine this crux diagram from the Forecasting Research Institute.

- Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) to indicate that their Responsible Scaling Policy now applies because they “observe or expect” a doubling of their research progress: Prior to this, Jack Clarke had commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027”
- Independent METR report on Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”.

(Source)

- METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information (TLDR: the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue) Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns (see below; source; METR further estimates that the uplift in rate of progress is only 1.7x if we limit it to that attributable to AI).

- Here’s the self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others.

- Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier. The benchmarks for Gemini 4 Carbon suggest that this strategy may have been effective.
- Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI.

- I found the Anthropic self-improvement report less useful, though, like the OpenAI report it also showed their engineers shipping about 8 times as much code. Limitations: This is a lot, but it’s hard to know how to correlate it with things that matter given how crude lines of code is as a measure. Engineers estimated the true output increase at 4 times. Of course, we might wonder how accurate subjective estimates actually are.

- A P-Zero Research study into AI’s research taste found; “the experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every ~3 months since December 2025. The best model, Opus 5.5, now exceeds our expert human baseline”. Limitations: “Our results may overstate how fast research taste is improving. Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb, and our human baseline doesn’t include top researchers, so it may significantly underestimate the performance of the best researchers in the world. TasteVal also doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on.”

## Are we sure?:

Next we’ll consider a tables from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lays out potential bottlenecks and fundamental limitations of AI:

Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Toby emphasises that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump (say from Mythos having been developed on top of a larger pre-train, which his results suggests scales better) rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x:

- Personally, progress has felt a lot faster in the last year. Honestly, I’m still kind of confused why a potential 2x speed increase seems to have been a big update for many people.

Is scaling issue an issue in practise? On the pro side, both Ramez Naam and Seb Krier note that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

On the con side, Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scales with inputs in such a way that it might be viable.

Dean Ball distinguishes between weak recursion and strong recursion:

- Weak recursion: “when a technology is a key input into the production of more and better versions of that same technology”. He describes this as, “the historical norm rather than an aberration“, describing ironsmiths using iron to make more iron and railways to transport the material needed to make more railways. He writes: ”weak recursion is not really weak: it is one of the most powerful dynamics in human history, rhyming if not synonymous with the concept of compounding growth. In the context of AI, weak recursion could result in a rapid increase in frontier AI capabilities—more rapid than anything we have seen so far—over the coming year or so.“
- Strong recursion: “when a technology can autonomously plan and execute the development of its successor”. He suggests it is never happened in history; even human brains haven’t yet achieved this. He writes: “strong recursion is a genuine risk, possibly in the near term, though the evidence for it is thinner than is sometimes supposed”. His case focuses particularly on long-range research taste: “Many of the most senior scientists in the field of deep learning, which undergirds all of modern AI, got into the field years or decades before it bore fruit. An empirical evaluation of their research taste would have shown these scientists to have quite poor taste, and quite low research productivity—right up until the deep learning revolution began in 2012”.

He acknowledges that there are ways for weak recursion to lead to strong recursion:

- Maybe “this characteristic we find so ineffable and mysterious will simply fall out of another round of scaling”
- Perhaps, “the capabilities acceleration that comes from weak recursion will yield models capable of strong recursion”
- Or maybe, “experimentation done at massive scale may be able to serve as a stand-in for taste” or at least ‘blur the boundaries“

He acknowledges these as possibilities, but he doesn’t take any of these as obviously true.

Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? provides us with some evidence in favour of Dean’s perspective. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. This provides some evidence that the issue of taste that Dean highlighted might be the bottleneck, though as Dean pointed out, this doesn’t show that this bottleneck will remain intractable.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response:

Well, this report finding acceleration of AI progress inside of Anthropic certainly has my attention! Digging in now before commenting much publicly.  Thanks all who pointed me to it.

In his original post, he wrote that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks. It’s interesting that Anthropic claims to have almost achieved this with an average self-reported uplift of only 12x. I wonder what explains this discrepency.

We previously saw that Arvind Narayanan expects any RSI to be narrow. Richard Ngo agrees that we should expect jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts”. Nonetheless, unlike Arvind he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects”:

- My take (assign this a low-weight as forecasting isn't really my area): I think it’s more likely than not that progress in the short-term will primarily be in domains that are more verifiable, with limited progress in domains that are less verifiable (which is what we have been seeing recently). That said, I would be surprised if this trend of limited progress in non-verifiable domains was robust into the medium term. Different options for utilising AI progress to feed back into itself become viable at different capability levels and non-verifiable domains remaining mostly intractable would require that none of these allow dramatic progress. Given that we have experienced a period where dramatic, general AI progress was possible (the pre-training era), we shouldn’t discount this as something that never happens.

## If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting the METR results forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes: If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

- “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
- “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

Samuel Hammond takes a very aggressive view of what RSI would mean:

In the pre-RSI regime, human frictions created automatic buffers between new model releases, giving researchers and society time to probe emergent capabilities, design better evals, develop novel alignment techniques, and adapt / harden their infrastructure. As progress has accelerated, capability improvements have already started outstripping our adaptive capacity, as manifest in METR's inability to evaluate model autonomy beyond 13 hours, and narrow window for cyber defenders to prepare for open weight versions of Mythos.

RSI will exacerbate all these issues and create all new ones.

At minimum, we should anticipate:

- the equivalent of a GPT-5.2 -> 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months),
- concurrent algorithmic improvements densifying models to ultra-efficient sizes at any given capability level
- 100x Mythos-like capabilities across most verifiable domains, including chem, nuclear and bio
- new forms of multi-agent misalignment risk
- "company in a box" agents trained to stand-up whole organizations / corporations
- "cyber nuke"-like capabilities that require de minimis infra
- several transformer-scale breakthroughs, such as for long-term memory / continual learning, open-ended domains, and/or all-new training techniques for idealized "GPT-zero"-esque metalearners
- concurrent speedups in any complementary technical domain, i.e. explosive rates of R&D and novel discoveries

Note that Samuel claims: “The equivalent of a GPT-5.2 → 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months)“. Why? His answer:

If you do a simple linear regression on model release cadence it predicts a new frontier model will be produced roughly every day by January 2027. Whether a daily release cadence makes any sense is another question. By that point I suspect new models will be private by default.

Wouldn’t the training runs take a certain amount of time even if the research itself is automated? I’d love to see his answer to this question.

Now might be a good time to share this Deepmind table on fundamental limitations:

Next we’ll go to the more sophisticated analysis from the AI Futures project that Ben Todd was referencing. Here’s what their model (published July 10 2026; ie. developed before the most recent results) predicted take-off to look like if we decided to allow the companies to race to ASI (“Plan D”):

In contrast, they proposed that we should attempt pace the rate of progress and they modelled this as follows:

How has the AI Futures project updated since?:

Daniel has said that he is “spooked" by this information.

Here's their updated forecasts (as a reminder: SAR = Superhuman AI Researcher and TED-AI = Top-Expert Dominating AI):

## Navigating RSI:

### Are we in triage mode?

In We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety, Miles Brundage argues:

“At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)

(This reading was previously part of the AISF governance course. I was sad to see it go)

Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. Miles wrote this post in February of this year (2026), I dig more into where he might have been coming from in my full notes on his article, but I’m skipping that here as the discourse has moved on from where it was back in February.

I’ll now share some counter-perspectives (keep in mind that some of these takes were written a while back).

Firstly, Richard Ngo worries that the AI safety community is overly focused on short-timelines:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

Eliezer Yudkowsky would undoubtedly be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive:

- “But isn’t this obvious!?” — he is making the point that people often quote a year named by an expert without realising how broad their timelines actually are.
- Is Toby Ord correct that many people are too confident about timelines being short, or does his stance come out of a lack in confidence? Taking a step back, what virtue does the current moment most call for: boldness or level-headedness?
- I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines.
- It would be interesting to know whether the named figures have narrowed their forecasts since then now that we know a lot more now than we did at the time.

Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby:

I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).

Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “radical optionality” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course). Of course, one must ask, are we still in the regime where radical optionality makes sense or are we past that now?

I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later.

Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context. I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll likely be Substack only; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate.

Take-off Speed:

In Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me, Ajeya describes three scenarios:

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)“. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips”

How should we characterise progress up until now?

Eliezer writes:

If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience.

Tom Davidson responded:

If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that

For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”.

“Bumpy” intelligence explosions

Forethought defines an additional scenario. For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs.

(Modified version of Forethought diagram.)

In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Elsewhere they’ve framed this as jaggedness applying not just to capabilities, but also to rate of change.

(Modified version of Forethought diagram.)

Delving into the weeds

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speeds is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Complicating matters further, if someone talks about short-timelines to AGI, it matters hugely whether they mean human-level intelligence (like some researchers have argued that we have already achieved) or whether they mean a system that is strongly capable of autonomously learning and improving itself. As Ajeya notes, someone might have short-timelines to AGI and then a slow-take off from there, or they might believe that things will move very fast once we’ve achieved the AGI milestone. A fast take-off post-AGI is much more likely if we mean the latter definition.

Of course, whether a “take-off” is fast or slow may depend on when we start counting from. Do we start counting from ChatGPT/GPT4 or only when we hit a particular AGI milestone? I think it’s useful to have the concept of a take-off that is slow then fast (argument in favour: perhaps there’s a phase transition when AI starts to feed back into its own development, argument against: improvements in AI-assisted development might be continuous and required simply to maintain the previous pace in light of decreasing marginal returns).

Feedback loops

The previous section focused primarily on what RSI might look like in terms of outputs, this section focuses on what kind of feedback loop might be driving this.

Types of “Intelligence Explosion”:

Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops:

Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion:

  • software only recursive self-improvement
  • AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design,
  • full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips.

The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff.

We already saw their model of how these different feedback loops could combine depending on the strength of each. I imagine they would have moved a reasonable amount of their probability mass from the “gradual” world to either “rapid” or “bumpy”.

They observe that the feedback loops could be divided further:

Indeed, the AI Futures model focuses on the possibility of a software intelligence explosion and distinguishes automating coding from automating research.

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

  • Automated Coder (AC). An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
  • Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR): A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete. Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).
  • Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI): A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.
  • Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

AI as a normal technology argues that the slowness of diffusion cycles will provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

Source

Projecting Trends into the Future

Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly, when we should be thinking exponentially”

This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view.

In some cases, the s-curves stack into an exponential:

Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish):

He also also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward):

Connor Leahry writes: “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty.

Are we experiencing RSI?

Before considering the evidence, it may make sense to examine this crux diagram from the Forecasting Research Institute.

  • Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) to indicate that their Responsible Scaling Policy now applies because they “observe or expect” a doubling of their research progress: Prior to this, Jack Clarke had commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027”
  • Independent METR report on Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”.

(Source)

  • METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information (TLDR: the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue) Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns (see below; source; METR further estimates that the uplift in rate of progress is only 1.7x if we limit it to that attributable to AI).
  • Here’s the self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others.
  • Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier. The benchmarks for Gemini 4 Carbon suggest that this strategy may have been effective.
  • Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI.
  • I found the Anthropic self-improvement report less useful, though, like the OpenAI report it also showed their engineers shipping about 8 times as much code. Limitations: This is a lot, but it’s hard to know how to correlate it with things that matter given how crude lines of code is as a measure. Engineers estimated the true output increase at 4 times. Of course, we might wonder how accurate subjective estimates actually are.
  • A P-Zero Research study into AI’s research taste found; “the experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every ~3 months since December 2025. The best model, Opus 5.5, now exceeds our expert human baseline”. Limitations: “Our results may overstate how fast research taste is improving. Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb, and our human baseline doesn’t include top researchers, so it may significantly underestimate the performance of the best researchers in the world. TasteVal also doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on.”

Are we sure?:

Next we’ll consider a tables from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lays out potential bottlenecks and fundamental limitations of AI:

Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Toby emphasises that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump (say from Mythos having been developed on top of a larger pre-train, which his results suggests scales better) rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x:

  • Personally, progress has felt a lot faster in the last year. Honestly, I’m still kind of confused why a potential 2x speed increase seems to have been a big update for many people.

Is scaling issue an issue in practise? On the pro side, both Ramez Naam and Seb Krier note that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

On the con side, Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scales with inputs in such a way that it might be viable.

Dean Ball distinguishes between weak recursion and strong recursion:

  • Weak recursion: “when a technology is a key input into the production of more and better versions of that same technology”. He describes this as, “the historical norm rather than an aberration“, describing ironsmiths using iron to make more iron and railways to transport the material needed to make more railways. He writes: ”weak recursion is not really weak: it is one of the most powerful dynamics in human history, rhyming if not synonymous with the concept of compounding growth. In the context of AI, weak recursion could result in a rapid increase in frontier AI capabilities—more rapid than anything we have seen so far—over the coming year or so.“
  • Strong recursion: “when a technology can autonomously plan and execute the development of its successor”. He suggests it is never happened in history; even human brains haven’t yet achieved this. He writes: “strong recursion is a genuine risk, possibly in the near term, though the evidence for it is thinner than is sometimes supposed”. His case focuses particularly on long-range research taste: “Many of the most senior scientists in the field of deep learning, which undergirds all of modern AI, got into the field years or decades before it bore fruit. An empirical evaluation of their research taste would have shown these scientists to have quite poor taste, and quite low research productivity—right up until the deep learning revolution began in 2012”.

He acknowledges that there are ways for weak recursion to lead to strong recursion:

  • Maybe “this characteristic we find so ineffable and mysterious will simply fall out of another round of scaling”
  • Perhaps, “the capabilities acceleration that comes from weak recursion will yield models capable of strong recursion”
  • Or maybe, “experimentation done at massive scale may be able to serve as a stand-in for taste” or at least ‘blur the boundaries“

He acknowledges these as possibilities, but he doesn’t take any of these as obviously true.

Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? provides us with some evidence in favour of Dean’s perspective. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. This provides some evidence that the issue of taste that Dean highlighted might be the bottleneck, though as Dean pointed out, this doesn’t show that this bottleneck will remain intractable.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response:

Well, this report finding acceleration of AI progress inside of Anthropic certainly has my attention! Digging in now before commenting much publicly. Thanks all who pointed me to it.

In his original post, he wrote that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks. It’s interesting that Anthropic claims to have almost achieved this with an average self-reported uplift of only 12x. I wonder what explains this discrepency.

We previously saw that Arvind Narayanan expects any RSI to be narrow. Richard Ngo agrees that we should expect jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts”. Nonetheless, unlike Arvind he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects”:

  • My take (assign this a low-weight as forecasting isn't really my area): I think it’s more likely than not that progress in the short-term will primarily be in domains that are more verifiable, with limited progress in domains that are less verifiable (which is what we have been seeing recently). That said, I would be surprised if this trend of limited progress in non-verifiable domains was robust into the medium term. Different options for utilising AI progress to feed back into itself become viable at different capability levels and non-verifiable domains remaining mostly intractable would require that none of these allow dramatic progress. Given that we have experienced a period where dramatic, general AI progress was possible (the pre-training era), we shouldn’t discount this as something that never happens.

If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting the METR results forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes: If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

  • “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
  • “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

Samuel Hammond takes a very aggressive view of what RSI would mean:

In the pre-RSI regime, human frictions created automatic buffers between new model releases, giving researchers and society time to probe emergent capabilities, design better evals, develop novel alignment techniques, and adapt / harden their infrastructure. As progress has accelerated, capability improvements have already started outstripping our adaptive capacity, as manifest in METR's inability to evaluate model autonomy beyond 13 hours, and narrow window for cyber defenders to prepare for open weight versions of Mythos.

RSI will exacerbate all these issues and create all new ones.

At minimum, we should anticipate:

  • the equivalent of a GPT-5.2 -> 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months),
  • concurrent algorithmic improvements densifying models to ultra-efficient sizes at any given capability level
  • 100x Mythos-like capabilities across most verifiable domains, including chem, nuclear and bio
  • new forms of multi-agent misalignment risk
  • "company in a box" agents trained to stand-up whole organizations / corporations
  • "cyber nuke"-like capabilities that require de minimis infra
  • several transformer-scale breakthroughs, such as for long-term memory / continual learning, open-ended domains, and/or all-new training techniques for idealized "GPT-zero"-esque metalearners
  • concurrent speedups in any complementary technical domain, i.e. explosive rates of R&D and novel discoveries

Note that Samuel claims: “The equivalent of a GPT-5.2 → 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months)“. Why? His answer:

If you do a simple linear regression on model release cadence it predicts a new frontier model will be produced roughly every day by January 2027. Whether a daily release cadence makes any sense is another question. By that point I suspect new models will be private by default.

Wouldn’t the training runs take a certain amount of time even if the research itself is automated? I’d love to see his answer to this question.

Now might be a good time to share this Deepmind table on fundamental limitations:

Next we’ll go to the more sophisticated analysis from the AI Futures project that Ben Todd was referencing. Here’s what their model (published July 10 2026; ie. developed before the most recent results) predicted take-off to look like if we decided to allow the companies to race to ASI (“Plan D”):

In contrast, they proposed that we should attempt pace the rate of progress and they modelled this as follows:

How has the AI Futures project updated since?:

Daniel has said that he is “spooked" by this information.

Here's their updated forecasts (as a reminder: SAR = Superhuman AI Researcher and TED-AI = Top-Expert Dominating AI):

Navigating RSI:

Are we in triage mode?

In We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety, Miles Brundage argues:

“At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)

(This reading was previously part of the AISF governance course. I was sad to see it go)

Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. Miles wrote this post in February of this year (2026), I dig more into where he might have been coming from in my full notes on his article, but I’m skipping that here as the discourse has moved on from where it was back in February.

I’ll now share some counter-perspectives (keep in mind that some of these takes were written a while back).

Firstly, Richard Ngo worries that the AI safety community is overly focused on short-timelines:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

Eliezer Yudkowsky would undoubtedly be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive:

  • “But isn’t this obvious!?” — he is making the point that people often quote a year named by an expert without realising how broad their timelines actually are.
  • Is Toby Ord correct that many people are too confident about timelines being short, or does his stance come out of a lack in confidence? Taking a step back, what virtue does the current moment most call for: boldness or level-headedness?
  • I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines.
  • It would be interesting to know whether the named figures have narrowed their forecasts since then now that we know a lot more now than we did at the time.

items.title: Would you let an AI judge you?
items.content:
Legal AI may outperform human lawyers on some benchmarks, but could an AI ever outperform a human judge? Judges don’t just argue rules, they interpret them and sometimes make new ones! As a result, autonomous judges are a microcosm of the alignment problem with potentially large societal impacts and costs.

My parent's dreams - like every other Jewish parent - may soon perish. Their two favorite professions, lawyers and doctors, could be fully replaced by AI in our lifetimes.

Beyond AI tools for professionals (Harvey/OpenEvidence), there’s a wave of AI native companies (Crosby/Nolla Health) that empower AIs to autonomously provide legal or medical services without any human supervision. In July, Crosby announced they were “taking out professional liability insurance for [their] agents, so that they can do autonomous legal work,” and Nolla Health became “the first organization in the U.S. authorized by a state regulator for AI to issue an initial prescription.”

While still early, the Crosby/Nolla type of firm are fundamentally different from the Harvey/OpenEvidence firms: they threaten to remove humans from the loop. This may not happen immediately - there are regulatory hurdles to jump through even when AI capabilities surpass that of humans - but it seems clear there’s a possibility AI lawyers and doctors fully replace humans in the medium-ish term (3-10 years).

If you don’t agree, then I suggest you stop reading here. The rest of this article will build on that assumption and only go further off the deep end. It will also focus on the legal half of this equation, because I am a mere Juris Doctor, not a Doctor of Medicine.

If you’re still here, I have a question for you: if you were arrested for a crime and put on trial, would you rather have a human lawyer or an equally effective AI lawyer?...
