items.content_html:
Legal AI may outperform human lawyers on some benchmarks, but could an AI ever outperform a human judge? Judges don’t just argue rules, they interpret them and sometimes make new ones! As a result, autonomous judges are a microcosm of the alignment problem with potentially large societal impacts and costs.

My parent's dreams - like every other Jewish parent - may soon perish. Their two favorite professions, lawyers and doctors, could be fully replaced by AI in our lifetimes.

Beyond AI tools for professionals (Harvey/OpenEvidence), there’s a wave of AI native companies (Crosby/Nolla Health) that empower AIs to autonomously provide legal or medical services without any human supervision. In July, Crosby announced they were “taking out professional liability insurance for [their] agents, so that they can do autonomous legal work,” and Nolla Health became “the first organization in the U.S. authorized by a state regulator for AI to issue an initial prescription.”

While still early, the Crosby/Nolla type of firm are fundamentally different from the Harvey/OpenEvidence firms: they threaten to remove humans from the loop. This may not happen immediately - there are regulatory hurdles to jump through even when AI capabilities surpass that of humans - but it seems clear there’s a possibility AI lawyers and doctors fully replace humans in the medium-ish term (3-10 years).

If you don’t agree, then I suggest you stop reading here. The rest of this article will build on that assumption and only go further off the deep end. It will also focus on the legal half of this equation, because I am a mere Juris Doctor, not a Doctor of Medicine.

If you’re still here, I have a question for you: if you were arrested for a crime and put on trial, would you rather have a human lawyer or an equally effective AI lawyer?...

items.title: Lightcone Commons' funders (and SFF and CG) are mostly NOT funding things that will prevent our extinction
items.content:
Lightcone Commons have completed their first granting round. And the things their granters and recommenders have funded mostly do not meet the current moment (the same is true for SFF’s most recent round, and Coefficient Giving). Let’s hope that their upcoming future rounds do better, or other funders step in. All of our lives are on the line.

(Apologies if this is blunt, but this is important..)

I get that money allocators (grantmakers and VCs alike) typically invest in people over ideas. But this is taking that to the extreme. Yudkowsky and Soares’ funding recommendations don’t fit with their book (which I am a big fan of)! They are funding obscure content creators, researchers and think tanks that are mostly just people in their Bay Area social circles, it seems. Why aren’t they funding orgs directly aimed at getting international agreement to ban RSI and ASI, as per what they say is necessary (and is, in fact, necessary), in chapter 14 of IABIED? I heard that orgs such as Control AI were in their funding orders, but why so low as to not have any real chance of being seriously funded?[1] Soares talks about organisations he’d recommend funding here, but is seemingly unaware that they already exist[2]. The other evaluators’ choices don’t seem any better (but at least some of them have excuses). $813k for Mox, $300k for Vibecamp, and only $75k for PauseIA [France] and $50k for PauseAI UK? (None for PauseAI Global or PauseAI US?) Seriously?

Other good grants: Stop The AI Race ($400k[3]); CeSIA ($765k); Secure AI project ($858k); American Shield ($1M). And on the margin, it’s good that campaign group Encode AI was given $2M, but they don’t even mention extinction risk on their website![4]

We need to be funding orgs that are consistent in warning of extinction risk, and how close we are to it. Most of the funded orgs don’t. Indeed, most mainstream media outlets now mention extinction more than AI Safety org websites!...

items.title: My tentative plans given less than one year left to change course [Linkpost]
items.content:
Subtitle: This mad race must end.

Note: I think this is partially me working through my plans and partially my emotions, so imo it's less epistemically rigorous than ideal for LessWrong.

I might have less than a year left to affect the insane, reckless, Faustian race to ASI, and I plan to spend that time doing everything I can to push for a pause.

I currently think there’s a decently high chance that by default, there’s 6-12 months left before my personal point of no return: the point after which my own actions no longer plausibly affect the future. This is different from other people’s points of no return: for example, people like Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic) or Donald Trump may have slightly longer times to wake up and change course. This is also different from other timelines that people sometimes throw around, like timelines to AGI or ASI or fully automated remote-worker or whatever. However, it is the most important for my own decisions.

I do not defend this position here. Other people have written partial explanations that I like (Karthik, AI Futures Project, Sentinel, Rutger Bregman). I may also write more accessible explainers in the near future.

Regardless, humanity is absolutely not ready for what comes next, whether that’s human extinction, complete loss of control to rogue AIs or a few oligarchs, or something far weirder.

While I don’t have strong confidence that I actually only have 6-12 months left, I think very few people are working on this by default, and AI Safety is growing very quickly (though still far smaller than needed), and newcomers to the field can cover the scenarios where we have more time.

Given this, I think my best strategy is to push hard for a pause on training AI: specifically a complete moratorium on training stronger AI models than the ones we currently have and severe limitations on AI R&D, until scientists, policymakers, and the general public have more time to understand what’s going on and catch up....

items.title: Staying sane when the world isn't
items.content:
This is a written version of a workshop I gave at EAG NYC in October 2026, edited to make sense in article form. Other materials: Slides with narrated audio, slides without audio, handout.

## Introduction

"In war, what in ordinary times would be thought weirdly zealous becomes expected...For do-gooders, it is always wartime." - Strangers Drowning

I'm opening with this quote because I want to hold in mind that many people reading this are working under a mentality of high urgency.

The EA atmosphere has felt different to me since Hugging Face and the sea change in existential risk discourse. I know that for lots of us the times do not feel normal.

So this piece is about how to be more okay in abnormal times. It’s for anyone working under chronic urgency or moral demandingness - especially people working on x-risk, or anything else tethered to rapid advancements in AI. But in my experience the same themes apply to other cause areas too.

This isn’t about specific mental health problems, and I don’t assume readers have any. Instead I hope to persuade you that sanity and sustainability are nonnegotiables for all of us; to share some perspective from working as an EA therapist; and help you start planning for ongoing stability.

### Where are you starting from?

Let's check where you're starting from. On the one hand, someone in a constant sprint at the edge of burnout who's doing nothing to care for themself should pause and sleep and probably make a plan for handoff.

But at the other end, sustainability isn't our only priority. At a certain point, adding more exercise (or fun, or rest) starts trading off against stuff we care about more.

So where we want to be is in the green, where we're putting our capacity to good use while also getting the full benefits of sustainability....

items.title: Positive and Negative AI Futures
items.content:
I'm continuing to share some notes I created for myself to use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I really like using Ilya: the AI scientist shaping the world as a way of engaging students at the start of a course. The video primarily focuses on the way that AI could go wrong, however, it also starts with “Now, AI is a great thing…”, so it naturally leads to a discussion of positive and negative futures.

Positive Futures:

- One obvious resource on positive futures Foresight Institute’s Existential Hope website. I’ve browsed their content in the past, some of it is kind of interesting, but honestly, I found view it as mostly pretty mid. They also run a fellowship which has an existential hope stream:
- They recently released The AI future nobody is showing you, which resulted in a wide range of reactions on Twitter. I think this is worth commenting on as it illustrates the challenges with attempting to produce a positive vision. Honestly, I’ve become quite pessimistic here: the gap between what different groups in society want may simply be too wide for it to be possible to find a positive vision that unites society: Steven Pinker was positive: “A more plausible vision, in my view, than either Utopia or doom.” Nikola Jurkovic was in the middle: “I admire the effort… but sadly this story falls into the common narrative trap of just assuming that AGI won’t actually be deployed widely.” @HellenicVibes hated it: “Wow how exciting to have a thousand years under the boot of ‘community leaders,’ ‘impacted minorities,’ and ‘AI auditors!’ I would literally rather be turned into paperclips.”
- Would it matter if there doesn’t exist a unifying positive vision? What’s wrong with different people having different visions of a positive future? Well, I wouldn’t say anything is wrong with people having different visions per se, but I suspect it makes navigating the path forward much harder, even if everyone broadly agrees that certain outcomes would be bad (I generally buy Yuval Harari’s argument that narratives play a crucial role in large-scale co-ordination): Patrick Collison writes: “I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario… We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.”
- Whilst Dario wrote Machines of Loving Grace that argued most people were under-estimating the update he has also argued that the public’s current negative perception of AI is unlikely to shift in response to messaging (“a glitzy marketing campaign”). He argues that it is fundamentally a matter of trust with the causes going back decades. What matters is not talking about curing cancer, but “actually curing cancer” or other diseases.
- Forethought has a series on Better Futures which argues that Flourishing is currently underrated relative to surviving on the basis of scale and neglectedness. I think the series should actually be called “Best Futures” as that’s his true focus, largely as a result of his (mostly) risk-neutral stance. There is also a course, though “Better Futures work” is something of a misnomer as that implies more distinctness from standard x-risk/catastrophic risk work than there is given that the Better Futures perspective only makes most such work more important on the margin.

Negative Futures:

- It’s worth remembering that the Ilya video started with him saying, “Now, AI is a great thing…” Of course, by the time you get to the end of the video and you’ve heard all the ways this can go wrong, it’s very easy to forget that he said that and reduce him to a “doomer” when he actually believes that AI can be built safely.
- Dario has complained about this phenomenon too. In response to criticism that he should be “more of a positive advocate for his own industry”, Dario has claimed that his messaging has been “equally balanced between risks and benefits” and that people may be misunderstanding his views because negative clips are disproportionately likely to go viral.
- In There’s No Rule That Says We Make it, Rob Miles claims that people often have an implicit belief that humanity will “rise to the occasion” even if they wouldn’t actually endorse that statement. He suggests that this may derive from fiction, where we face challenges, but we almost always overcome then. He dismisses this fictional “evidence” as not real evidence. Whilst Rob is talking about existential risk, you could apply his argument more broadly to less severe risks as well.

Intermediate Futures:

Utopia or dystopia certainly aren’t the only two possibilities. There’s also the chance of an intermediate path and I wanted to mention it here for balance since most of the material in the course will stand in opposition to this perspective. One particularly prominent perspective in this vein is AI as a Normal Technology: “Transformative economic and societal impacts will be slow (on the timescale of decades)… We do not think that viewing AI as a humanlike intelligence is currently accurate or useful for understanding its societal impacts, nor is it likely to be in our vision of the (foreseeable) future (their timescale here is vague, but they concede that their view “has failed and/or is no longer useful” if “strong AI” is “developed and deployed in the next decade”).” (summary, guide, critique by AI Futures Project, common ground, viral music video critique “Thus Spoke Compute”).

Their project has three elements:

- A description of current AI
- A prediction about the foreseeable future
- A prescription about how we should respond

(I have an instinctual reaction that using a single catchy phrase “AI as a Normal Technology” as a framework for answering three separate questions feels “too neat”. I acknowledge that simplicity is a virtue of an analytical framework andI admit this is a shallow objection, but nonetheless I do see this as a yellow flag).

Additional detail:

- They have a three stage model of technological progress: invention, innovation and diffusion. They argue things will move slowly as further invention often requires additional learnings or data which can only come from iteratively diffusing/deploying the technology. They believe this process will take decades rather than years and that improvements in AI improvements can only accelerate this so much because the diffusion loop sets an overall “speed limit”. Key crux: can AI can contract the decades of diffusion by deploying itself or would the speed limit remain due to social factors, delays for testing models or repeated waits for data to be collected?

- Their view centres resilience over alignment (inherently brittle, requires models to have context which we might not want to give them) or non-proliferation (infeasible, brittle, increases correlated failures via market concentration, limits defensive use, not justified for speculative risks). “Attempting to make an AI model that cannot be misused is like trying to make a computer that cannot be used for bad things. Model-level safety controls will either be too restrictive (preventing beneficial uses) or will be ineffective against adversaries who can repurpose seemingly benign capabilities for harmful ends.”
- They also argued against focusing too much on catastrophic misalignment due to the risk being speculative (they argue that these probabilities are insufficiently grounded to form the basis of public policy).

It’s natural to wonder where they stand post-Hugging Face. They have a post:

- They believe that many of their claims have “held up”, however they acknowledge making a few mistakes: “We did not pay sufficient attention to safety risks that arise during development and evaluation (as opposed to the widespread deployment of models)“: Lawrence Chan has argued AI models can be dangerous before public deployment. On that point Chernobyl was actually the result of a safety test (a post-deployment safety test, but still!) “We were too confident that companies would take basic control precautions”: They write: “our expectation was that existing legal liability, imperfect as it is, and the risk of brand damage would be a sufficient antidote to such organizational practices. We were wrong. This reinforces the need for policy interventions” “And underplayed the importance of jaggedness which led us to underestimate how quickly capabilities could improve in domains such as cybersecurity”: They write that jaggedness applies doesn’t just apply to the level of capabilities, but also the rate of change: “Thus, we are no longer confident in our earlier prediction that the offense-defense balance will continue to hold even with advances in AI.”
- They nonetheless argue don’t accept the Hugging Face incident as a discontinuity, instead taking it as evidence of smaller incidents occurring before large: “The harms that resulted from these attacks are many, many orders of magnitude smaller than other AI harms we already tolerate”: Note that their position is more subtle than continuity simply being automatic: “We have emphasized that we can and must engineer continuity rather than take it for granted”
- They argue that known technical and organisational control could have prevented the Hugging Face incident and have been neglected by the AI safety community: “We should assume every model will be capable of escape and self-reproduction. Safety shouldn’t rely on that being difficult.” This doesn’t mean that they think existing techniques are sufficient (they wonder why cybersecurity researchers haven’t “seized this moment with gusto”).
- They claim that cyberrisk is the only real urgent AI threat because it is unusual in two ways: “in that superhuman capabilities are even possible, and because it is a purely digital risk with no physical-world bottleneck.”

My perspective:

I think they make many quite interesting points, though I do find the “AI as a Normal Technology” label frustrating. Honestly, I wish they’d pursued this project in the following way:

- Define what a normal technology view of AI looks like.
- Define what an abnormal technology view of AI look like.
- Discuss the extent to which current AI is a normal technology and the extent to which it is an abnormal technology.
- Discuss the extent to which they expect this trend will hold going forward.

If they had positioned it as a lens instead of a comprehensive world view, I expect that they could have uplifted the discourse. Instead, it often ends up being debated as a binary yes or no, with the public debate being further muddied by their use of “Normal Technology” significantly differing from casual usage. That said, naming is hard and it’s arguably unfair to blame them for other people latching onto their article in order to defend an oversimplified normal technology perspective. Many people dislike how “AI safety” often refers exclusively to catastrophic or existential risks and whilst I tend to use this term in the way they dislike, I see their frustration as completely reasonsable.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

Discuss

The author expresses pessimism about the very possibility of a shared positive vision.
items.content_html:
I'm continuing to share some notes I created for myself to use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I really like using Ilya: the AI scientist shaping the world as a way of engaging students at the start of a course. The video primarily focuses on the way that AI could go wrong, however, it also starts with “Now, AI is a great thing…”, so it naturally leads to a discussion of positive and negative futures.

Positive Futures:

  • One obvious resource on positive futures Foresight Institute’s Existential Hope website. I’ve browsed their content in the past, some of it is kind of interesting, but honestly, I found view it as mostly pretty mid. They also run a fellowship which has an existential hope stream:
  • They recently released The AI future nobody is showing you, which resulted in a wide range of reactions on Twitter. I think this is worth commenting on as it illustrates the challenges with attempting to produce a positive vision. Honestly, I’ve become quite pessimistic here: the gap between what different groups in society want may simply be too wide for it to be possible to find a positive vision that unites society: Steven Pinker was positive: “A more plausible vision, in my view, than either Utopia or doom.” Nikola Jurkovic was in the middle: “I admire the effort… but sadly this story falls into the common narrative trap of just assuming that AGI won’t actually be deployed widely.” @HellenicVibes hated it: “Wow how exciting to have a thousand years under the boot of ‘community leaders,’ ‘impacted minorities,’ and ‘AI auditors!’ I would literally rather be turned into paperclips.”
  • Would it matter if there doesn’t exist a unifying positive vision? What’s wrong with different people having different visions of a positive future? Well, I wouldn’t say anything is wrong with people having different visions per se, but I suspect it makes navigating the path forward much harder, even if everyone broadly agrees that certain outcomes would be bad (I generally buy Yuval Harari’s argument that narratives play a crucial role in large-scale co-ordination): Patrick Collison writes: “I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario… We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.”
  • Whilst Dario wrote Machines of Loving Grace that argued most people were under-estimating the update he has also argued that the public’s current negative perception of AI is unlikely to shift in response to messaging (“a glitzy marketing campaign”). He argues that it is fundamentally a matter of trust with the causes going back decades. What matters is not talking about curing cancer, but “actually curing cancer” or other diseases.
  • Forethought has a series on Better Futures which argues that Flourishing is currently underrated relative to surviving on the basis of scale and neglectedness. I think the series should actually be called “Best Futures” as that’s his true focus, largely as a result of his (mostly) risk-neutral stance. There is also a course, though “Better Futures work” is something of a misnomer as that implies more distinctness from standard x-risk/catastrophic risk work than there is given that the Better Futures perspective only makes most such work more important on the margin.

Negative Futures:

  • It’s worth remembering that the Ilya video started with him saying, “Now, AI is a great thing…” Of course, by the time you get to the end of the video and you’ve heard all the ways this can go wrong, it’s very easy to forget that he said that and reduce him to a “doomer” when he actually believes that AI can be built safely.
  • Dario has complained about this phenomenon too. In response to criticism that he should be “more of a positive advocate for his own industry”, Dario has claimed that his messaging has been “equally balanced between risks and benefits” and that people may be misunderstanding his views because negative clips are disproportionately likely to go viral.
  • In There’s No Rule That Says We Make it, Rob Miles claims that people often have an implicit belief that humanity will “rise to the occasion” even if they wouldn’t actually endorse that statement. He suggests that this may derive from fiction, where we face challenges, but we almost always overcome then. He dismisses this fictional “evidence” as not real evidence. Whilst Rob is talking about existential risk, you could apply his argument more broadly to less severe risks as well.

Intermediate Futures:

Utopia or dystopia certainly aren’t the only two possibilities. There’s also the chance of an intermediate path and I wanted to mention it here for balance since most of the material in the course will stand in opposition to this perspective. One particularly prominent perspective in this vein is AI as a Normal Technology: “Transformative economic and societal impacts will be slow (on the timescale of decades)… We do not think that viewing AI as a humanlike intelligence is currently accurate or useful for understanding its societal impacts, nor is it likely to be in our vision of the (foreseeable) future (their timescale here is vague, but they concede that their view “has failed and/or is no longer useful” if “strong AI” is “developed and deployed in the next decade”).” (summary, guide, critique by AI Futures Project, common ground, viral music video critique “Thus Spoke Compute”).

Their project has three elements:

  • A description of current AI
  • A prediction about the foreseeable future
  • A prescription about how we should respond

(I have an instinctual reaction that using a single catchy phrase “AI as a Normal Technology” as a framework for answering three separate questions feels “too neat”. I acknowledge that simplicity is a virtue of an analytical framework andI admit this is a shallow objection, but nonetheless I do see this as a yellow flag).

Additional detail:

  • They have a three stage model of technological progress: invention, innovation and diffusion. They argue things will move slowly as further invention often requires additional learnings or data which can only come from iteratively diffusing/deploying the technology. They believe this process will take decades rather than years and that improvements in AI improvements can only accelerate this so much because the diffusion loop sets an overall “speed limit”. Key crux: can AI can contract the decades of diffusion by deploying itself or would the speed limit remain due to social factors, delays for testing models or repeated waits for data to be collected?
  • Their view centres resilience over alignment (inherently brittle, requires models to have context which we might not want to give them) or non-proliferation (infeasible, brittle, increases correlated failures via market concentration, limits defensive use, not justified for speculative risks). “Attempting to make an AI model that cannot be misused is like trying to make a computer that cannot be used for bad things. Model-level safety controls will either be too restrictive (preventing beneficial uses) or will be ineffective against adversaries who can repurpose seemingly benign capabilities for harmful ends.”
  • They also argued against focusing too much on catastrophic misalignment due to the risk being speculative (they argue that these probabilities are insufficiently grounded to form the basis of public policy).

It’s natural to wonder where they stand post-Hugging Face. They have a post:

  • They believe that many of their claims have “held up”, however they acknowledge making a few mistakes: “We did not pay sufficient attention to safety risks that arise during development and evaluation (as opposed to the widespread deployment of models)“: Lawrence Chan has argued AI models can be dangerous before public deployment. On that point Chernobyl was actually the result of a safety test (a post-deployment safety test, but still!) “We were too confident that companies would take basic control precautions”: They write: “our expectation was that existing legal liability, imperfect as it is, and the risk of brand damage would be a sufficient antidote to such organizational practices. We were wrong. This reinforces the need for policy interventions” “And underplayed the importance of jaggedness which led us to underestimate how quickly capabilities could improve in domains such as cybersecurity”: They write that jaggedness applies doesn’t just apply to the level of capabilities, but also the rate of change: “Thus, we are no longer confident in our earlier prediction that the offense-defense balance will continue to hold even with advances in AI.”
  • They nonetheless argue don’t accept the Hugging Face incident as a discontinuity, instead taking it as evidence of smaller incidents occurring before large: “The harms that resulted from these attacks are many, many orders of magnitude smaller than other AI harms we already tolerate”: Note that their position is more subtle than continuity simply being automatic: “We have emphasized that we can and must engineer continuity rather than take it for granted”
  • They argue that known technical and organisational control could have prevented the Hugging Face incident and have been neglected by the AI safety community: “We should assume every model will be capable of escape and self-reproduction. Safety shouldn’t rely on that being difficult.” This doesn’t mean that they think existing techniques are sufficient (they wonder why cybersecurity researchers haven’t “seized this moment with gusto”).
  • They claim that cyberrisk is the only real urgent AI threat because it is unusual in two ways: “in that superhuman capabilities are even possible, and because it is a purely digital risk with no physical-world bottleneck.”

My perspective:

I think they make many quite interesting points, though I do find the “AI as a Normal Technology” label frustrating. Honestly, I wish they’d pursued this project in the following way:

  • Define what a normal technology view of AI looks like.
  • Define what an abnormal technology view of AI look like.
  • Discuss the extent to which current AI is a normal technology and the extent to which it is an abnormal technology.
  • Discuss the extent to which they expect this trend will hold going forward.

If they had positioned it as a lens instead of a comprehensive world view, I expect that they could have uplifted the discourse. Instead, it often ends up being debated as a binary yes or no, with the public debate being further muddied by their use of “Normal Technology” significantly differing from casual usage. That said, naming is hard and it’s arguably unfair to blame them for other people latching onto their article in order to defend an oversimplified normal technology perspective. Many people dislike how “AI safety” often refers exclusively to catastrophic or existential risks and whilst I tend to use this term in the way they dislike, I see their frustration as completely reasonsable.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

Discuss

items.title: The Epicurean technique of meeting claims with more claims
items.content:
In Epicurus's letter to Pythocles, he proposes three different explanations for lightning strikes: compression of air by wind, a cloud suddenly breaking, or a buildup of fire suddenly bursting.

All wrong, but he goes on to say (Makridis translation):

It is indeed possible that the thunderbolt may be generated in any one of many more ways.

Maybe this is all you need if you're annoyed with people saying it's Zeus's wrath so you'd better make sacrifices at their temple.
You just have to say, well, it could be a lot of other things too.

## Meeting unfounded explanations with more explanations

I used to think you shouldn't propose explanations without evidence.
Now I think you should have at least three.
If you come up with an explanation that's total speculation or pseudoscience, don't feel bad for making unfounded claims.
Think of two more.

Or if someone else proposes some bullshit explanation, it's more fun to come up with new explanations than to complain about a lack of evidence.
But more importantly, that's what it means to lack evidence, right?
We know there's no evidence when we can propose alternatives, and there's no evidence that falsifies them.

I do sometimes propose alternatives adversarially, when I'm annoyed, as Epicurus was, at the unfounded claims of others.
When I say you lack evidence, the content of my claim is that you cannot rule out other plausible alternatives.
The right way to make that case, at least in my opinion, is directly: list the alternatives.
Everything else (you haven't done a study, or you did a study but it wasn't randomized, etc.) is at best a proxy for this substance.

But, again, it's fun to propose explanations.
When someone isn't taking what they're saying too seriously, I think I should meet them in the same spirit and play the same game.

## Recognizing evidence by the possibilities it excludes

Of course, sometimes a claim is well-founded after all....

items.title: Additional Course Context (for AI Safety Fundamentals; unofficial)
items.content:
Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content—not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest.

Some general thoughts on advice

I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another.

In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?).

Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear. People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less.

(See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom: “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”)

Some thoughts on frameworks

People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few.

I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions.

Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them.

The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown?

Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made.

This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice.

Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes: “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.”

Cruxes when attempting to predict the future:

- Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)?
- Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results?
- Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward).

“AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”:

I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course:

- If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed: Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to? Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence.
- Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “ early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system ” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper. These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence. Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AGI paper provides a helpful performance × generality matrix (attached), however given that capabilities appear more jagged than the ChatGPT days, I would personally want to add a third column in between narrow and general.

- One of the most famous definitions of AGI (technically whether machines can “think”) is the Turing Test. A 2026 paper by Jones and Bergen observed LLMs (GPT 4.5 and Llama) that were prompted to act like humans successfully passed a three-way Turing test, as per Turing’s original setup, where an interrogator is interviewing two agents: one human and one AI. This setup is more difficult to pass because the interrogator can directly compare the two and because they don’t need to guess the base rate. The interrogators were given 5 minutes (matching the duration mentioned in Turing’s paper, though this was only by way of example, rather a specification). These interrogators were drawn from two subsets: students and a company called Prolific (Turing only spoke of “average” interrogators). Some people have criticised this paper on the basis that some of the interrogators didn’t seem to try that hard. Whilst impressive, it’s worth noting that this kind of linguistic imitation is arguably precisely what LLMs are made for, in which case we should expect their performance here to be much less indicative of their general abilities than if AI had been produced another way.
- In A Definition of AGI (Oct 2025), Hendrycks et al. attempt to define AGI using Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, “the most empirically validated model of human cognition”. They write, “”AGI is an AI that can match or exceed the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult”. However, whilst this model is verified as providing a robust categorisation of intellectual abilities in humans, it doesn’t automatically mean that these categories are suitable for AI, especially since artificial intelligence is often spiky in ways that feels utterly bizarre to humans.

- Dario isn’t really a fan of the term as he believes there’s no clear boundary between AGI and non-AGI. One analogy I like: if you’re on a road trip from San Fransisco to New York and someone wants to know how long it’ll be, it initially doesn’t matter very much whether you’re headed to New York state or New York city (or which neighbour in New York), but as you get closer, the precise definition becomes much more important. Helen Toner makes more or less the same argument using fuzzy clouds in concept space: “it had a good run”. On the other hand, Sam Altman shares these worries but has resigned himself to the term’s popularity: “the word seems so sticky, I gave up trying to fight it”.

My top recommendation for better understanding where we are now: Honestly, I need to find a new one (I would appreciate suggestions!). I was previously recommending What the hell happened with AGI Timelines in 2026? to my previous cohort, where Rob Wiblin attempted to synthesize a lot of different data into a coherent view:

- For example, he listed “AI does some original math” as ambiguous. OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed. There’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data, but they also dropped 372 other results onto the internet (yet to be verified; some of these have Lean proofs, but it is possible to make a mistake in how a problem is formalised). Frontier Math Tier 4 has also been saturated.

- He also said that time horizons were on trend. Time horizons now appear remarkably above trend (note the error bars though!) One critique that gained a lot of attention was How to game the METR plot. It observed that there were only 14 samples in the 1-4 hour range and that the limited diversity of tasks would make it very easy for a lab to game, even without training on the test set. METR has responded to this criticism and others.

- Counterpoint: Toby Ord has argued that inference-time compute scales less favourably than you might expect. Many folk have missed the fact that certain linear seeming graphs actually have a log-scale on the x-axis

General Trends:

- BlueDot’s 2 hour Future of AI course contains a lot of information on this. I’ve attached a picture showing the progress in image models and a graph showing the amount of money being invested.

- A diagram from Epoch’s Trends in Artificial Intelligence show the current rate of progress of various components of AI

- A frequently cited, but somewhat old, diagram from Our World shows benchmarks saturating increasingly fast. Unfortunately, the benchmark situation seems to have become worse recently.

Scale of Societal Impact:

The Technological Richter Scale: This tools allows you to calibrate the predicted impact of AI against other technologies.

MirrorCode and Emergent Abilities

Fable 5 achieved a substantial advance on MirrorCode (64% vs. 20% for GPT 5.6 Sol), a benchmark involving reimplementing an entire program end-to-end:

- Unfortunately, I haven’t had time to look into this benchmark in detail, but it really made me stop and think because it makes the rapid upwards trend on METR time horizons feel much more plausible to me. The METR time horizons have absurdly large error bars, as well as having been subject to various criticisms; whilst I didn’t necessarily didn’t believe their results, I effectively had them down as a “maybe, who knows” in my mind. Seeing the rapid advance in MirrorCode makes we wonder, “Wait, should I be believing the METR’s most recent results? Because if so, that would be huge!”
- It’s worth noting that the benchmark requires a 100% test pass rate in order to pass an individual task. The fact that it uses such a strongly binary scoring system helps explain how it was possible for progress on this benchmark to take-off so quickly. As Boaz Barak observes, if completing a task really means completing a number of tasks of similar difficulty successfully, then the success curve tends to end up being much steeper.

- This ties directly into the question of emergent abilities: many folks have observed cases where capabilities have rather suddenly emerged as training scaled. However, Schaffer et al have suggested that this is a mirage as the emergence phenomena depends on the specific metric researchers observe.

- Boaz counters that even if there is a metric according to which an ability was just following the trend, this is only helpful if we know that this is the right metric in advance. If we don’t know how to decompose a task into “simpler predictable components”, then we may still experience capability increases as more or less emergent.
- This isn’t just a theoretical question. The capabilities of Mythos seem to have caught many people by surprise (note how quickly the Trump administration swapped from voluntary to “voluntary” evaluation of frontier models). As mentioned in Setting the Scene the graph showing CVEs is wild. Some people expected this, most did not.

- The extent to which the capabilities or impacts of models can be predicted in advance affects the degree to which evals should be central to the way companies and broader society approach the issue of safety. Institutions want to be able to produce legible schemes of regulation as it reduces their reliance of subjective judgement. Sometimes this is possible, other times this only produces false assurance.

Take-off Speeds:

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)”. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” (from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me).

Forethought defines an additional scenario: a “bumpy” intelligence explosion. More on this later, but one way this could happen would be if AI progress feeds back into developing better models for a while, but it then becomes bottlenecked (perhaps because the loop is longer for AI to recursively improve the chips we use to run and train it or maybe because we need to fully automate chip production)

Two older definitions (mostly defunct; included for historical reasons):

- Vernor Vinge: Soft = years; hard = “very short period of time”, perhaps less than 100 hours
- Eliezer Yudkowsky: Fast = weeks or hours vs. years or decades

Timelines

It’s worth being aware that when people talk about AI timelines they’re often imagining very different milestones. Given the difficultly of predicting the future, we might not want to be place too much confidence in our predictions:

- I’ve included a table from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lists four potential paths from AGI to ASI (artificial superintelligence).

- Current Metaculus predictions are September 2027 for weakly general AI and Nov 2030 for a stronger definition of general AI to be developed and publicly announced. However, it’s hard to know how much we should trust prediction markets on questions regarding transformative technologies as they haven’t been around for that long (Metaculus was founded in 2015).
- The AI Futures model (an update of the AI 2027 model) currently predicts automated coding around October 2027 (operationalised as an AI that would be as productive on its own as only human coders with no AIs; guidance on research taste is still provided by humans) and superintelligence around December 2028 (defined as the gap between the AI and the best humans is twice the gap between the best humans and the median professional on virtually all cognitive tasks). There forecasts tend to be on the more aggressive side, but less so than their previous work; many frontier lab employees, or other folks in the Bay area, now seem to be expecting similar rates of progress. As of August 2026, they felt that AI was moving at 70-90% of the rate they’d predicted in AI 2027.

- Frontier Lab Predictions: In June 2026, Dario wrote: “If these scaling laws continue for only a year or two longer, we are likely to get what I’ve called Powerful AI, or “a country of geniuses in a datacenter”“. Jack Clark recently declared that the singularity has begun. Time reported that Sam Altman said that OpenAI was “not quite yet” there, but “by the end of the year (2026) the company would have an internal system he would call AGI”. Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content—not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest.

Some general thoughts on advice

I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another.

In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?).

Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear. People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less.

(See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom: “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”)

Some thoughts on frameworks

People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few.

I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions.

Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them.

The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown?

Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made.

This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice.

Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes: “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.”

Cruxes when attempting to predict the future:

  • Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)?
  • Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results?
  • Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward).

“AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”:

I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course:

  • If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed: Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to? Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence.
  • Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “ early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system ” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper. These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence. Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AGI paper provides a helpful performance × generality matrix (attached), however given that capabilities appear more jagged than the ChatGPT days, I would personally want to add a third column in between narrow and general.
  • One of the most famous definitions of AGI (technically whether machines can “think”) is the Turing Test. A 2026 paper by Jones and Bergen observed LLMs (GPT 4.5 and Llama) that were prompted to act like humans successfully passed a three-way Turing test, as per Turing’s original setup, where an interrogator is interviewing two agents: one human and one AI. This setup is more difficult to pass because the interrogator can directly compare the two and because they don’t need to guess the base rate. The interrogators were given 5 minutes (matching the duration mentioned in Turing’s paper, though this was only by way of example, rather a specification). These interrogators were drawn from two subsets: students and a company called Prolific (Turing only spoke of “average” interrogators). Some people have criticised this paper on the basis that some of the interrogators didn’t seem to try that hard. Whilst impressive, it’s worth noting that this kind of linguistic imitation is arguably precisely what LLMs are made for, in which case we should expect their performance here to be much less indicative of their general abilities than if AI had been produced another way.
  • In A Definition of AGI (Oct 2025), Hendrycks et al. attempt to define AGI using Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, “the most empirically validated model of human cognition”. They write, “”AGI is an AI that can match or exceed the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult”. However, whilst this model is verified as providing a robust categorisation of intellectual abilities in humans, it doesn’t automatically mean that these categories are suitable for AI, especially since artificial intelligence is often spiky in ways that feels utterly bizarre to humans.
  • Dario isn’t really a fan of the term as he believes there’s no clear boundary between AGI and non-AGI. One analogy I like: if you’re on a road trip from San Fransisco to New York and someone wants to know how long it’ll be, it initially doesn’t matter very much whether you’re headed to New York state or New York city (or which neighbour in New York), but as you get closer, the precise definition becomes much more important. Helen Toner makes more or less the same argument using fuzzy clouds in concept space: “it had a good run”. On the other hand, Sam Altman shares these worries but has resigned himself to the term’s popularity: “the word seems so sticky, I gave up trying to fight it”.

My top recommendation for better understanding where we are now: Honestly, I need to find a new one (I would appreciate suggestions!). I was previously recommending What the hell happened with AGI Timelines in 2026? to my previous cohort, where Rob Wiblin attempted to synthesize a lot of different data into a coherent view:

  • For example, he listed “AI does some original math” as ambiguous. OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed. There’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data, but they also dropped 372 other results onto the internet (yet to be verified; some of these have Lean proofs, but it is possible to make a mistake in how a problem is formalised). Frontier Math Tier 4 has also been saturated.
  • He also said that time horizons were on trend. Time horizons now appear remarkably above trend (note the error bars though!) One critique that gained a lot of attention was How to game the METR plot. It observed that there were only 14 samples in the 1-4 hour range and that the limited diversity of tasks would make it very easy for a lab to game, even without training on the test set. METR has responded to this criticism and others.
  • Counterpoint: Toby Ord has argued that inference-time compute scales less favourably than you might expect. Many folk have missed the fact that certain linear seeming graphs actually have a log-scale on the x-axis

General Trends:

  • BlueDot’s 2 hour Future of AI course contains a lot of information on this. I’ve attached a picture showing the progress in image models and a graph showing the amount of money being invested.
  • A diagram from Epoch’s Trends in Artificial Intelligence show the current rate of progress of various components of AI
  • A frequently cited, but somewhat old, diagram from Our World shows benchmarks saturating increasingly fast. Unfortunately, the benchmark situation seems to have become worse recently.

Scale of Societal Impact:

The Technological Richter Scale: This tools allows you to calibrate the predicted impact of AI against other technologies.

MirrorCode and Emergent Abilities

Fable 5 achieved a substantial advance on MirrorCode (64% vs. 20% for GPT 5.6 Sol), a benchmark involving reimplementing an entire program end-to-end:

  • Unfortunately, I haven’t had time to look into this benchmark in detail, but it really made me stop and think because it makes the rapid upwards trend on METR time horizons feel much more plausible to me. The METR time horizons have absurdly large error bars, as well as having been subject to various criticisms; whilst I didn’t necessarily didn’t believe their results, I effectively had them down as a “maybe, who knows” in my mind. Seeing the rapid advance in MirrorCode makes we wonder, “Wait, should I be believing the METR’s most recent results? Because if so, that would be huge!”
  • It’s worth noting that the benchmark requires a 100% test pass rate in order to pass an individual task. The fact that it uses such a strongly binary scoring system helps explain how it was possible for progress on this benchmark to take-off so quickly. As Boaz Barak observes, if completing a task really means completing a number of tasks of similar difficulty successfully, then the success curve tends to end up being much steeper.
  • This ties directly into the question of emergent abilities: many folks have observed cases where capabilities have rather suddenly emerged as training scaled. However, Schaffer et al have suggested that this is a mirage as the emergence phenomena depends on the specific metric researchers observe.
  • Boaz counters that even if there is a metric according to which an ability was just following the trend, this is only helpful if we know that this is the right metric in advance. If we don’t know how to decompose a task into “simpler predictable components”, then we may still experience capability increases as more or less emergent.
  • This isn’t just a theoretical question. The capabilities of Mythos seem to have caught many people by surprise (note how quickly the Trump administration swapped from voluntary to “voluntary” evaluation of frontier models). As mentioned in Setting the Scene the graph showing CVEs is wild. Some people expected this, most did not.
  • The extent to which the capabilities or impacts of models can be predicted in advance affects the degree to which evals should be central to the way companies and broader society approach the issue of safety. Institutions want to be able to produce legible schemes of regulation as it reduces their reliance of subjective judgement. Sometimes this is possible, other times this only produces false assurance.

Take-off Speeds:

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)”. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” (from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me).

Forethought defines an additional scenario: a “bumpy” intelligence explosion. More on this later, but one way this could happen would be if AI progress feeds back into developing better models for a while, but it then becomes bottlenecked (perhaps because the loop is longer for AI to recursively improve the chips we use to run and train it or maybe because we need to fully automate chip production)

Two older definitions (mostly defunct; included for historical reasons):

  • Vernor Vinge: Soft = years; hard = “very short period of time”, perhaps less than 100 hours
  • Eliezer Yudkowsky: Fast = weeks or hours vs. years or decades

Timelines

It’s worth being aware that when people talk about AI timelines they’re often imagining very different milestones. Given the difficultly of predicting the future, we might not want to be place too much confidence in our predictions:

  • I’ve included a table from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lists four potential paths from AGI to ASI (artificial superintelligence).
  • Current Metaculus predictions are September 2027 for weakly general AI and Nov 2030 for a stronger definition of general AI to be developed and publicly announced. However, it’s hard to know how much we should trust prediction markets on questions regarding transformative technologies as they haven’t been around for that long (Metaculus was founded in 2015).
  • The AI Futures model (an update of the AI 2027 model) currently predicts automated coding around October 2027 (operationalised as an AI that would be as productive on its own as only human coders with no AIs; guidance on research taste is still provided by humans) and superintelligence around December 2028 (defined as the gap between the AI and the best humans is twice the gap between the best humans and the median professional on virtually all cognitive tasks). There forecasts tend to be on the more aggressive side, but less so than their previous work; many frontier lab employees, or other folks in the Bay area, now seem to be expecting similar rates of progress. As of August 2026, they felt that AI was moving at 70-90% of the rate they’d predicted in AI 2027.
  • Frontier Lab Predictions: In June 2026, Dario wrote: “If these scaling laws continue for only a year or two longer, we are likely to get what I’ve called Powerful AI, or “a country of geniuses in a datacenter”“. items.title: WOKE feminist EXPOSES left-wing anti-meme (NOT CLICKBAIT)
items.content:
content warning: discussion of abusive relationships

Some ideas are memetic: they're catchy, they spread widely and easily, people have a reaction to them that induce them to propagate them further. Others are anti-memetic: for whatever reason, they have naturally self-censoring tendencies that reduce their reach.

My grandmother was a late-in-life convert to Christianity, who dragged the rest of the family along for a bit. I was an earnest, credulous bookworm of eight or so, and I took the youth pastor at his word when he encouraged all of us to read more of the bible in our own time. As it turns out, the youth pastor is actually not thrilled when you do, and come back with inconvenient questions. Parts of the bible can be anti-memetic in some Christian circles.

A bit later, I found myself in very socially progressive circles. I was an earnest, credulous bookworm of eighteen or so, who took the community leaders at their word when they told us that it is important to read theory, but even more important to do direct work and listen to the oppressed when their viewpoints diverged from the theory (which was written by dead white men). This I spent my early career doing, first at a remove at domestic violence policy summits and deep inside the federal public service, and then more directly at food banks and homeless shelters. I care deeply about improving the world, and I learned much about the kinds of work that are required to bring about the healed one. However, I did not disclose much of my learnings at the anarchist potlucks and communist reading groups. I somehow knew that they would not make me especially popular....

items.title: Novel togetherness and CEV: My unconventional path from Whitehead to alignment
items.content:
“Bringing in the sheaves,” Wake of the Flood, Rick Griffin

This post (my first) shares reflections on how I got here (LW) and where I plan to go next, mainly by way of briefly exploring a few philosophical perspectives that brought me to alignment topics. If nothing else, hopefully I can provide one example of someone who is reading LW in 2026 from a perspective outside the AI zeitgeist.

## An outsider’s perspective on CEV

To the best of my current understanding, my terminal values include (among others) self-awareness, self-determination, community, healthy diversity, compassion, and fun.

Although perhaps unorthodox, my personal view of CEV emphasizes the distinction between what is coherent across humanity and what remains ineffably individual, especially to the extent that individuality is necessary for relationship among a multiplicity of selves. I roughly follow a vision articulated (with plenty of stated uncertainty and dated quirks) by Robert Hunter (Grateful Dead lyricist) in a long-forgotten email chain[1] using the metaphor of “bringing in the sheaves,” a sort of ritual gathering of humanity’s volition over time. The destruction of Hunter’s “healthy diversity” of selves, and the loss of I-thou relationships enabled by such diversity, is the prime risk that the singleton poses from my perspective. Such a reading has Hegelian foundations in the collapse of undifferentiated being into pure nothing without inner diversity or reference outwards (Science of Logic 1§132), though I recognize that my terminal value of relationships among selves is purely subjective....

items.title: Realize When You're Stupid
items.content:
[This post is the second post in my thirty day writing challenge. Tune in for more if you enjoy it!]

If you reliably knew that you would make a bad decision during a certain time, would you let yourself make decisions during that time? Probably not, right? So why do you let yourself grocery shop when hungry, speak negatively when you have low blood sugar, and make key decisions when anxious?

A core epistemic skill that I’ve tried to cultivate over the years is the idea of knowing when I’m stupid, and not letting myself make decisions during these times. Like all core epistemic skills, I’ve cultivated this in response to getting repeatedly smacked across the face over and over again.

I.

Cindy is an anxious woman. Her resting heart rate is a bit high, she gets wigged out easily, and she tends to run an endless stream of disaster loops through her head at all hours of the day. Like all anxious people, her anxiety rises and falls. Maybe it rises when her blood sugar is low, when she’s under-slept, or when other things in her life are particularly stressful. Probably all three.

She, like all people, has a number of decisions to make throughout the day. Some of these decisions are big and some of them are small. Cindy reliably finds that when she’s flooded with anxiety, she repeatedly runs into certain failure modes. For example, maybe she makes elaborate plans to fix every single problem in her entire life, half-commits to it for, like, one day, and then decides that: no, what was she thinking? That plan is terrible! It’s time for another ground-breaking, earth-shaking plan that will fix every single problem in her entire life. She then half-commits to this plan, and then one day later comes to a terrible realization.......

items.title: Psychologically Preparing for Short Timelines
items.content:
In response to recent news from METR on possible RSI and likely 1-3 year timelines, I am feeling it. Heaviness in my chest, watery eyes, the works. I realized I'm currently not psychologically prepared for the world to get crazier than it already has.[1]

I think most people reading this already know ~what's best for them and this post will mostly serve as a reminder. What follows is my current plan and advice for myself.

For me, the most important things are:

- Morning Routine
- Bedtime Routine
- Exercising
- Living meditation practice (ie throughout the day)

And the most important thing to NOT do is be on my phone/screens.

[Note on getting "stuck": if you do feel emotionally awful and no IFS/CBT seems to work, I recommend "How to Reset"]

## Morning Routine

I have a sunrise alarm clock (shines light to wake you up) and enjoy writing in the morning.

## Bedtime Routine

At 8:30 an alarm goes off, and I watch an episode of Empress in the Palace with my wife, then we get ready for bed. Also like to journal then.

## Exercising

Rock climbing some days & jogging to the bus stop

## Living Meditation Practice

There are 3 traits I'd like to cultivate more:

- Aliveness
- Gratitude
- Relaxation

For me, aliveness is about being aware of local-details that you're experience right now ("being present") and the extreme amount of options you have available to you. This can be painful (eg if I'm feeling a lot of pain), but I do have a choice on what my mind sticks to.

While typing this, I do notice my jaw & stomach are tense (so I automatically relaxed them) and my eye hurts (so I lowered the brightness). Noticing, for me, is most of the battle.

I shoudl have dedicated sessions for gratitude (ie gratitude journaling) and relaxation (for me, "doing nothing" is nice), but my main focus is making this a living practice: something I intentionally practice throughout the day....
